text: Rift Valley fever (RVF) is one of the major viral zoonoses in Africa, affecting humans and several domestic animal species. The epidemics in eastern Africa occur in a 5-15 year cycle coinciding with abnormally high rainfall generally associated to the warm phase of the El Niño event. However, recently, evidence has been gathered of inter-epidemic transmission. An open-source, easily applicable, accessible and modifiable model was built to simulate the transmission dynamics of RVF. The model was calibrated using data collected in the Kilombero Valley in Tanzania with people and cattle as host species and Ædes mcintoshi, Æ. ægypti and two Culex species as vectors. Simulations were run over a period of 27 years using standard parameter values derived from two previous studies in this region. Our model predicts low-level transmission of RVF, which is in line with epidemiological studies in this area. Emphasis in our simulation was put on both the dynamics and composition of vector populations in three ecological zones, in order to elucidate the respective roles played by different vector species: the model output did indicate the necessity of Culex involvement and also indicated that vertical transmission in Ædes mcintoshi may be underestimated. This model, being built with open-source software and with an easy-to-use interface, can be adapted by researchers and control program managers to their specific needs by plugging in new parameters relevant to their situation and locality.

text:
Comparison of changes in body composition, adipokines and inflammatory markers after initial therapy with a nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (N(t)RTI)- sparing or containing regimen are scarce.

Randomised Clinical Trial.

This is the body composition substudy of NEAT 001/ANRS 143, a randomised trial comparing darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) plus either raltegravir (RAL) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) in 805 ART naïve HIV-infected adults. The primary endpoint was percentage change in limb fat at week 96. Secondary endpoints were associations among these changes and metabolic markers (IL-6, insulin, leptin, adiponectin, FGF-23).

126 subjects (61 DRV/r + RAL and 65 DRV/r + TDF/FTC) were included. The rate of change in BMI between groups for RAL versus TDF/FTC at week 96 was 1.5% per 48-week period (p = 0.015). The rate of change in limb fat mass, trunk fat mass, total body fat and total lean mass was for RAL versus TDF/FTC at week 96 was 2.5% (p = 0.38), 7.3% ((p = 0.021), 4.9% (p = 0.061) and 1.3% (p = 0.12) respectively. Baseline insulin and leptin levels were correlated with baseline limb fat and trunk fat mass [r = 0.31 (p = 0.0043)/r = 0.28 (p = 0.0011) for limb fat, and r = 0.63 (p<0.0001)/r = 0.50(p<0.0001) for trunk fat]. After adjustment, a 10% faster increase in leptin between baseline and week 48 was associated with a more rapid increase in limb fat at week 48 (0.5% per 48 weeks, p<0.001), total body fat mass (0.6% per 48 weeks, p<0.001), and trunk fat mass (0.3% per 48 weeks, p = 0.0026).

After week 96 a N(t)RTI sparing regimen of DRV/r + RAL produced a numerically greater percentage increase in body composition variables with only change in trunk fat mass and BMI being significant.

text:
Women’s ability to make decisions regarding their reproductive health has important implications for their health and well-being. We studied the socio-demographic factors affecting reproductive health decision-making among women in 27 sub-Sahara African countries.

The study made use of pooled data from current Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) conducted from January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2016 in 27 countries in sub-Sahara African. Binary and multivariate logistic regression models were used to investigate the associations of women’s socio-demographic factors with decision-making regarding sexual reproductive health.

The proportion of women who can ask their partners to use a condom during sexual intercourse ranged from lowest in Mali (16.6%) to highest in Namibia (93.4%). Furthermore, the proportion of women who can refuse sex ranged from 18.3% in Mali to 92.4% in Namibia. Overall, approximately every five out of ten women can ask their partners to use a condom, six out ten women could refuse their partners sex and seven out of ten women could make at least 1 decision. Women from rural areas (OR = 0.51, CI = 0.48–0.54), those with no education (OR = 0.11, CI = 0.10–0.12), Muslim women (OR = 0.29, CI = 0.27–0.31), women not working (OR = 0.53, CI = 0.51–0.56) and women whose partners had no education (OR = 0.17, CI = 0.16–0.19) were less likely to make a decision on their reproductive health.

Residence, age, level of education, religion, occupation and partner’s education were found to be associated with women’s decision-making about sexual intercourse, condom use and reproductive health decision-making index. This study contributes to the discourse on reproductive health decision-making in Africa. Policies and intervention targeted at improving women’s autonomy and empowering them to take charge of their sexual and reproductive health issues should be focused on these factors.

text: African populations are characterized by high degree of genetic diversity. This high genetic diversity could result from the natural selection pressure. Several studies have described an association between some genetic diversities and difference of susceptibility to infectious diseases like malaria. It seems therefore important to consider genetic diversity impact when interpreting results of clinical trials in malaria endemic areas. This study aimed to determine the genetic polymorphism with erythrocyte traits in different populations of malaria endemic area in Mali. The cross-sectional surveys were carried out in different ethnic groups living in malaria endemic areas in Mali. Six milliliters of whole blood were collected in EDTA vials from each participant after informed consent has been obtained. The ABO, RH, Kell, MNSs, Kidd and Duffy systems phenotypes were assessed by the technique of gel filtration. A total of 231 subjects were included from six villages. The blood groups phenotypes O (40.7%) and A (31.2%) were more frequent with respective allele frequencies of 0.65 and 0.21. In the RH system the haplotypes R0 (0.55), r (0.20) and R1 (0.13) were the most frequent. Seven percent (7%) of Duffy positive and 4% of Glycophorin B deficiency (S-s-) were observed among participants. All participants were Kell negative. ABO and RH systems were polymorphic in these ethnic groups in Mali. Their implication in susceptibility to malaria should be taken into account in clinical trials interpretation, and for prevention of blood transfusion risks during anemia frequently caused by malaria in children.

text:
Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that can occur in all warm-blooded animals, including humans. Vaccinating dogs can protect people from contracting rabies. Rabies is a public health threat in Rwanda, but the country does not have information on the epidemiology of rabies. The present study aimed to understand the knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) of rabies and its control among dog owners in Kigali city of Rwanda.

We conducted a cross-sectional survey using a structured questionnaire among 137 dog owners selected from nine administrative study sites. A two-stage random sampling procedure was used to select the participants. Frequency distributions analysis and a series of chi-square tests of associations as well as binary logistic regressions were performed to determine the important factors associated with the response variables.

The results showed that 99.5% of respondents knew at least a host susceptible to rabies. Only 22.4% and 21.3% knew that dogs and people can develop rabies, respectively. Nearly 73.6% knew that human rabies can be transmitted through dog-bites and 99% could identify at least a clinical sign of canine rabies. Overall, 81.8% knew that regular vaccination of dogs helps to prevent dog-transmitted human rabies and 43.1% and 26.3% were aware that rabies in humans and in dogs are fatal once clinical symptoms have shown, respectively. Only 69% would observe a dog for 10 days after it bites a man or an animal. Approximately 20.4% were familiar with appropriate cleaning of dog-bites wounds, and 20.6% knew that puppies could receive rabies vaccination before they are three months old. Of those who owned vaccinated dogs, 78% were happy about the cost (US $ ≤ 34) of rabies vaccination. Of all the respondents, 58% had their dogs vaccinated at home by veterinarians while 86% indicated their veterinarians kept rabies vaccines on ice in a cool box. Overall, 53% of the dog owners had sufficient knowledge of rabies, whilst 66% and 17% adopted adequate practices and positive attitudes towards rabies, respectively. Multivariable logistic regression analyses indicated that none of the respondents’ sex, educational level, and the length of dog ownership were statistically associated with their knowledge, attitudes and practices of rabies.

This study showed that majority of the dog owners had sufficient knowledge and adopted appropriate practices of rabies. However there exist some knowledge gaps among the dog owners particularly on treatment, transmission and control methods. Therefore, rabies awareness campaign is required to upgrade rabies knowledge of the dog owners on rabies prevention and control in Rwanda.

To assess the survival of patients with cervical cancer (CC). Since the recommendations concerning cervical cancer management adopted by Polish medical societies do not differ significantly from the ESGO or non-European guidelines, and the fact that evaluation of the system for CC treatment in Poland, as well as the mortality rate of Polish women with CC, which is 70% higher than the average for European Union (EU) countries, justifies the hypothesis that treatment of CC in Poland deviates from the Polish and international recommendations. This article puts forward the current management of cervical cancer in Poland and discusses it in the context of ASCO guidelines.

A survey retrospective multicenter analysis of the medical records of 1247 patients with cervical cancer who underwent treatment for disease and who had completed at least two years of follow-up.

Although concurrent radiotherapy and chemotherapy is a standard treatment of FIGO IB to IVA cervical cancer patients in enhanced- and maximum-resources settings, in our analysis, we found that the percentage of women subjected to chemotherapy was lower than in countries where total survival rates were lower.

Within the IA to II A cervical cancer patients studied group, the methods of treatment remained in line with ASCO guidelines for countries with the highest standard of care.

Although concurrent radiotherapy and chemotherapy is a standard treatment of FIGO IB to IVA cervical cancer patients in enhanced- and maximum-resources settings, in our analysis, we found that the percentage of women subjected to chemotherapy was lower than in countries where total survival rates were lower.

Our findings, together with the inconsistencies within the cervical cancer screening program, may be one of the explanations of poorer survival rate of women with cervical cancer in Poland.

We aimed to identify and evaluate the quality and evidence of the motor learning literature about intervention studies regarding the contextual interference (CI) effect (blocked vs. random practice order) in children with brain lesions and typically developing (TD) children.

Eight databases (Cinahl, Cochrane, Embase, PubMed, Pedro, PsycINFO, Scopus and Web of Knowledge) were searched systematically with predefined search terms. Controlled studies examining the CI effect in children (with brain lesions or TD) were included. Evidence level, conduct quality, and risk of bias were evaluated by two authors independently. A best evidence synthesis was performed.

Twenty-five papers evaluating TD children were included. One of these studies also assessed children with cerebral palsy. Evidence levels were I, II, or III. Conduct quality was low and the risk of bias high, due to methodological issues in the study designs or poor description thereof. Best evidence synthesis showed mainly no or conflicting evidence. Single tasks showed limited to moderate evidence supporting the CI effect in TD children.

There is a severe limitation of good-quality evidence about the CI effect in children who practice different tasks in one session, especially in children with brain lesions.

HSS works because sound of sufficiently high frequency above human hearing does not normally spread out like audible frequency waves. These waves can be projected onto specific individuals, causing them to hear a sound that appears to be emanating from themselves, while others around them hear nothing.

Potential benefits could include the reduction of noise pollution in public places. Announcements, instructions, and advertisements could be aimed at individuals, not disturbing their neighbors. People in the same room could all listen to different music without the use of headphones.

Crank up the volume, and HSS could also be useful to military or law enforcement agencies. HSS beams can be focused up to 500 yards away, transmitting warnings or temporarily stunning and disabling a person with non-lethal force.

The AirScooter™ is a flying, helicopter-like personal vehicle that is planned to be made available for sale later this year. The price is estimated to be less than US$50,000.

Weighing less than 300 pounds and able to carry a load of an additional 350 pounds, the AirScooter runs on ordinary gasoline rather than expensive airplane fuel, and is able to travel about 2 hours at 55 m.p.h. on a 5-gallon tank, at heights up to 10,000 feet above sea level. Its ultralight weight means that no pilot license is required to fly one.

The light weight is made possible by the production of a new AeroTwin 4-stroke engine specifically for the AirScooter, designed by motorcycle racing engine specialists at Pearson Motor Co of New Zealand. Stability is provided by two rotors both set on a single shaft, which turn in opposite directions, eliminating the need for a tail rotor.

The craft is steered using only the hands on a motorcycle-like handlebar. Throttle up to gain altitude, turn left or right to rotate, and move the bars like a joystick to steer in different directions, including reverse.

Pictures and video of the new craft are available from the AirScooter.com website.

Norris plans to use the prize money to establish a foundation to help other struggling, independent inventors like himself.

El Salvador has been suspended from competing in all world football internationals. FIFA, the governing body in football, suspended the Salvadorian Football Association (FESFUT) over government involvement. The Salvadorian government refused to recognise local football officials that FIFA had appointed.

Last year, the head of the Salvadorian Football Association, Rodrigo Calvo, resigned. FIFA stepped in and appointed a special commission to reform the finances of the association. However, Salvadorian president Mauricio Funes refused to recognize the commission. FIFA considered this political interference.

The suspension affects next month's World Cup in South Africa. Despite the national team not qualifying, three referees have been selected to participate in the tournament. If the suspension is not overturned by the start of the tournament, they will not be able to participate.

A meeting of an executive commission is due to take place on June 8; should the El Salvadorian government not change its stance on the issue, the suspension will be finalised. If the government does not change its stance, El Salvador will remain suspended for the entire year until the FIFA congress meets again in June 2011.

Ecuador created chances freely and kept Costa Rica quiet for a 3-0 victory in the AOL Arena, Hamburg, Thursday.

The win for the South American team meant both Ecuador and Germany, each with six points from two games, progressed from Group A into the knock-out phase of the Fifa World Cup in Germany.

It was a comfortable match for Ecuador's Columbian coach Luis Suarez. He managed to rest three key players - goal scorer Carlos Tenorio, provider Luis Valencia, and impressive centre-back Giovanny Espinoza, with substitutes before the game was out.

Ecuador played keep ball well and maintain a slow tempo while Alexandre Guimaraes's side did not look a team able to raise the pace of the game and sustain pressure on Christian Mora's goal.

The game-winner was scored after seven minutes of action. Valencia to the right of the penalty area whipped a ball across the goal. Tenorio, unmarked in front of Jose Porras, dipped his body and headed in.

Costa Rica and Ecuador both missed opportunities before half time: Douglas Sequeira was unmarked at the Ecuador far post but his header was mistimed and wide.

Then Edison Mendez and Agustin Delgado nearly combined for a carbon-copy of the first goal; but the striker, who had ran in unmarked in front of Porras, did stab at the ball and skewed it wide.

After he had another shot saved Degaldo's third attempt found the net. He shot hard from an angle inside the penalty area and beat Porras on his near post.

It was then Tenorio's substitute Kaviedes's turn to miss two then score one. A save from Porras, a header wide, and finally the striker connected for a beautiful far post volley, finishing off another Mendez cross.

Costa Rica were unlucky when a clever first time chip from Alvaro Saborio beat Mora only to hit a post but they had not created the clear chances that Ecuador had at the other end.

The long shots from Carlos Hernandez and Mauricio Solis's tricky run were acts of individual play. No match for a solid-looking team who got its second consecutive World Cup shut out and will play Germany for the honour of Group A winner, on June 20.

Standard & Poor's downgraded Egypt's currency rating for the second time in four months based on the country's shorfall in foreign reserves and shaky political transition. It's the latest development for a nation facing mounting economic diffuclties.

Egypt's foreign reserves fell by over 50 percent last year to about US$16 billion. Egypt has requested US$3.2 billion from the International Monetary Fund to bolster its reserves and prevent a devalation but that could take months.

Experts say that Egypt's problem of attracting foreign investment and tourists, which are two sources that would increase reserves, has already caused the Egyptian pound to lose 1 percent of its value and if the country doesn't solve the shortfall in foriegn currency, it could even lead to a further currency devaluation within the next two to three months.

The long-term solution is to restore tourism and foreign investments but both are suffering because of the continuing unrest.

Egyptian tourism suffered this past year as a result of a revolution, a transition to an elected government, and continuing signs of unrest and instability.

The Egyptian Revolution began on January 25 last year and President Hosni Mubarak resigned over two weeks later on February 11. The protests have continued as Egyptians grew uncomfortable with the military's control over the transition. At the start of this month, 79 people were killed at a soccer event in Port Said.

Tourism in Egypt accounted for US$12.5 billion in 2010 but fell 30 percent, or US$8.8 billion, in 2011, according to Mounir Fakhry Abdel Nour, Egypt's tourism minister. Tourism accounts for 11.6 percent of Egypt's GDP.

Last week, two U.S. female tourists and their Egyptian guide were abducted in the Sinai peninsula by Bedouin tribesmen and released shortly afterward.

The kidnapping took place in broad daylight on a busy road while the tourists travelled after a visit to St. Catherine's Monastery. Masked tribesmen stopped their bus, abducted the tourists by gunpoint, and escaped into the mountains. Three other tourists of unknown nationalities were left on the bus. Local authorities organized a search which ended in negotiations with local Bedouin tribesmen. The Bedouin demanded the release of recently apprehended tribesmen, who had been detained for drug trafficking and robbery. The US hostages were released unharmed, Abdel Nour said.

As a location, Egypt boasts ancient pyramids, the Nile River, Biblical sites like Mount Sinai, museums, and Red Sea coastal resorts. Last year the number of tourists plunged from fifteen million people down to nine million, which is a 40 percent drop.

Egypt's current investment climate is also severely hampered by the perception that the climate is not yet right for investment.

Mulyani Indrawati, managing director of the World Bank, said investors were not ready to get back into the markets of the Arab Spring countries until stability is restored but the situation has also been exacerbated by the precarious state of the regional and international economy.

text:
Egyptian businessman Hisham Talaat Moustafa, chairman of the construction and real estate firm Talaat Moustafa Group and a member of parliament for the ruling National Democratic Party, and former policeman Mohseen Al Sukkari have been convicted of murdering Lebanese pop star Suzanne Tamim.

The prosecution alleged that Mustafa, who had an affair with Tamim, paid Al Sukkari US$2 million to kill her. The woman was found dead in her Dubai apartment last July. Her throat was slit and she had suffered other stab wounds.

The pair's defense had been that evidence collected in the United Arab Emirates could have been tampered with and should not be used against them. The case was tried in Cairo due to the fact the arrests occurred in Egypt and took 27 hearings to reach a conviction.

Moustafa was stripped of parliamentary immunity after his September arrest and has been in jail since during his trial. He has stood down from his position within the Talaat Moustafa Group and his brother Tarek Talaat Moustafa now heads the company, which was founded by their father Talaat Moustafa.

text:
USGS reported that an earthquake struck the Dominican Republic region with a magnitude of 8.0. It was registered on last Friday at 01:38:55 a.m. (05:38:55 UTC) at the epicenter, which was located 102 km from Higüey, La Altagracia, Dominican Republic. However, it was later reported as a magnitude 3.4 earthquake by the Puerto Rico Seismic Network. The report caught the attention of the news media until the USGS reported it was 3.2.

The depth of the aftershock was located 89.8 km (55.8 mi), and no damage or injuries were reported. It has been reported as a Haiti aftershock.

The Haiti earthquake reached magnitude 7.0 Mw, with an epicentre near the town of Léogâne, almost 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) west of Port-au-Prince, the capital of Haiti. More than 100 aftershocks have been registered since that earthquake. The United Nations reported that the earthquake has caused more than 225,000 deaths, a number which is expected to rise.

Another earthquake of magnitude 5.3 hit the Kermadec Islands region. The epicenter was located 1,138 kilometers from Nuku'alofa, Tonga and had a depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles). It took place at 13:35:34 (01:35:34 UTC) at the epicenter. No tsunami warnings have been issued by NOAA for this earthquake.

A Japan earthquake took place in the Ryukyu Islands at 11:19:58 at epicenter (02:19:58 UTC). It reached a magnitude of 5.1, had a depth of 35 kilometers and the epicenter was located 80 kilometers from Naha, Okinawa.

text:
Those arrested were, according to the US government, members of a spy ring that had existed for several years, involving Russian agents adopting civilian identities. All are charged with acting as unlawful agents for Russia, which carries a sentence of a prison term up to five years. Nine were charged with money laundering, a crime that carries a prison term of up to twenty years.

According to the US government, the suspects had been trained by the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service to obtain information about US military policies, including those concerned with nuclear weapons, as well as intelligence about leadership at the CIA and the White House.

The FBI said that to obtain those objectives, the suspects were instructed to live as American citizens under false names, some as married couples. Some suspects were able to achieve ties with prominent US citizens, including a scientist working with nuclear weapons and a New York financier who had ties to officials within the US government.

Communication with Russian authorities was allegedly via several disparate methods, including unique wireless internet connections or pictures posted on the Internet with hidden messages, as well as more traditional methods such as burying messages or swapping bags between agents.

Names in quotes are cover names, while those not in quotes are real names of the alleged agents. Couples are on the same bullet, while those living alone are separate. Locations are where the suspects were arrested.

text:
A state of emergency was declared Sunday for the U.S. state of Washington by governor Christine Gregoire, as additional reports of storm-related casualties surfaced. The state National Guard has been deployed to aid in distributing supplies.

Thousands were still without power in the coastal and Puget Sound regions, though most urban areas were back with power as late as Sunday afternoon, and outages were mostly contained to rural and unincorporated areas. Puget Sound Energy reported that roughly 500,000 energy customers out of the 700,000 who lost power were back in service by Sunday evening. Seattle City Light, the city's independent municipal utility, reported only 18,000 customers still without power as of Monday morning, down from a peak of 175,000.

Four additional deaths related to the post-storm power outage had been reported as of Monday, bringing the total number of casualties to eight. A man in Gig Harbor was electrocuted by a downed power line while walking his dog. Another man in Spanaway died when an unattended candle caused a house fire.

On Monday, four new carbon-monoxide deaths were reported in a family of five in Burien due to an indoor generator. In Canada, which had some damage from the week's storms, two southern British Columbia carbon monoxide deaths were also reported. Despite continued warnings, hospitals are still seeing cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, including a family in w:Shoreline, Washington which was taken to the hospital after they reported symptoms due to their indoor grill. Neighbors of the Burien family suggested that noise concerns are leading people to place noisy generators indoors.

The Red Cross set up shelters throughout King and other affected counties for those without power or food. Hotels reported no vacancies as whole families took shelter in powered hotels, especially in Seattle. Restaurants also reported brisk business as people sought out a hot cooked meal. Tons of perishable food were expected to have become unsafe after the prolonged outage disabled refrigerators and freezers both in homes and stores.

Many of those without power visited nearby friends and family living where power had been continued or restored, while others traveled out of the area to places that had not been affected. The widespread outage made long-distance traveling treacherous on some major routes, with roadway lighting, cellular towers, and services disabled by the outage.

Most major roadways which were closed during the storm were reopened on Friday. The 520 Floating Bridge over Lake Washington, a major conduit to the technology-rich Eastside, sustained minor damage. Amtrak, which had halted its Cascades service, resumed Saturday evening. Sea-Tac Airport resumed operations with a reduced flight load, after a transient power outage on Friday disabled the airport radar and caused all planes to be grounded until it was repaired.

text:
A strong defensive display and two well taken goals saw Ecuador beat Poland in the second Group A match at the soccer World Cup.

The thousands of Polish fans who had traveled to the Veltins-Arena stadium in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, saw their team struggle to put together attacking plays.

Ecuador, whose captain and defender Ivan Hurtado was taken off injured on 67 minutes, scored a goal in the first half and one ten minutes from the end for a 2-0 victory.

The first twenty minutes was cagey with both sides unable to find form; there was not one chance on goal for the first twenty minutes.

When one did come it was Ecuador who capitalised: a throw-in from the right into the penalty area was flicked on for Carlos Tenario to nod passed the outstretched fingers of Artur Boruc into the far corner of the Polish net.

While first half-possession was equal for both sides Poland dominated the second period as Ecuador sat back on their lead, content to hit on the break.

Poland continued their early form of choosing the wrong pass and many times lost the ball in the third of the pitch nearest the opposition goal.

Ecuador scored a second ten minutes from time; in a rare attack near the Polish goal the ball was threaded by Polish defenders leaving a two on one with a stranded Boruc.

The Polish game never got going for manager Pawel Janas until the last five minutes when they hit the horizontal and then the vertical whitework of Christian Mora's goal.

Much of the credit for the performance of Luis Suarez's Ecuador side must be put at the feet of their defenders, particularly Giovanny Espinoza and Ivan Hurtado.

He will be hoping his defensive leader recovers for the next game against Costa Rica while Poland must contend with a German side who won their first game of the World Cup, Friday.

text:
During the first day of voting in Iraq elections, two suicide bombers have attacked polling stations in Baghdad, killing at least 14.

The attacks occurred during early voting in for the elections, which allow government employees, the sick and prisoners to vote ahead of the elections on Sunday. Two attacks occurred, about an hour apart, in different districts of Baghdad. According to the official count, at least 14 people died in the attacks, not counting attacks the day before that killed 31 people. Unofficially, reports from the scene of the attacks suggested that these counts were significantly less than the actual toll. According to officials, the attacks were carried out by insurgents trying to disrupt the elections, which are seen as a pivotal event in Iraq's attempts to unify the country.

In preparation for the elections, and in response to the threats posed by the insurgents, the Iraqi government has undertaken substantial security efforts, including extensive planning for the event, as well as working with American military forces. Despite the preparations, a senior official within the government acknowledged the threat of violence, saying that until a stable government is formed, the potential for further attacks still exists.

text:
Charlie, the novel's adolescent narrator, adopts the alias of the same name as he embarks on his freshman year of high school. The story unfolds through letters he writes to an unnamed friend, someone he's heard girls at school speak of fondly. Charlie's anticipation is tempered by anxiety, largely due to the recent suicide of his only close friend, Michael. Feeling isolated from his parents and older siblings, who never truly grasped who he was, Charlie finds solace in memories of his Aunt Helen, the sole relative he ever felt truly connected to. Tragically, she died in a car accident on his seventh birthday.

Throughout the novel, Charlie strikes up a friendship with two seniors, Sam and her step-brother Patrick. Alongside his English teacher, Bill, they expose Charlie to a myriad of new experiences, all chronicled in his letters, which chart his personal growth. Charlie recounts his adventures with his new friends: party escapades, attending and performing in the Rocky Horror Picture Show, and his first date. He also explores the complexities of love, both his unrequited feelings for Sam and a brief romance with Mary Elizabeth, another friend in their circle.

The narrative also delves into Patrick's secret relationship with Brad, the football team's quarterback, who is grappling with his own sexuality. Additionally, Charlie's sister's abusive relationship becomes a poignant subplot, resonating with Charlie due to his Aunt Helen's history of abuse. As the summer draws to a close, Charlie's journey culminates in a symbolic moment: standing in the truck bed as Patrick and Sam lead him through the tunnel, a stark contrast to his initial fearful experience. Through these experiences, Charlie learns to embrace life, unshaken by fear, realizing his role as a wallflower—a silent observer who finally steps into the light.

text:
This study sought to assess the quality and evidence base of motor learning literature pertaining to contextual interference (CI) effect, comparing blocked versus random practice order, in children with brain lesions and typically developing (TD) children.

A systematic search was conducted across eight databases (Cinahl, Cochrane, Embase, PubMed, Pedro, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Knowledge) using predefined search terms. Included studies were controlled investigations of the CI effect in children, either with brain lesions or TD. Two authors independently evaluated evidence level, study conduct quality, and risk of bias. A best evidence synthesis was performed.

Twenty-five papers involving TD children were included, with one study also assessing children with cerebral palsy. Evidence levels ranged from I to III. However, overall conduct quality was low, and risk of bias was high, primarily due to methodological flaws or inadequate study descriptions. Best evidence synthesis revealed largely no or conflicting evidence, with single tasks demonstrating limited to moderate support for the CI effect in TD children.

High-quality evidence regarding the CI effect in children practicing multiple tasks within a session is notably lacking, particularly for children with brain lesions.

text: Rift Valley fever (RVF) is a significant viral zoonosis in Africa, impacting humans and various domestic animals. In eastern Africa, outbreaks follow a 5-15 year cycle, often linked to high rainfall during the warm phase of El Niño events. However, recent findings suggest inter-epidemic transmission also occurs. To understand these dynamics, a model was developed using open-source software. text:
Rabies poses a significant public health risk in Rwanda, and while the country lacks comprehensive epidemiological data, understanding the knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) surrounding rabies among dog owners is crucial. This study sought to investigate these factors within Kigali city.

A cross-sectional survey was conducted using a structured questionnaire among 137 dog owners, randomly selected from nine administrative areas. Data were analyzed using frequency distributions, chi-square tests, and binary logistic regressions to identify key factors associated with the response variables.

The findings revealed that nearly all respondents (99.5%) were aware of at least one animal susceptible to rabies. However, knowledge gaps existed regarding specific susceptible animals, with only 22.4% recognizing dogs and 21.3% recognizing humans as susceptible. While 73.6% knew that human rabies can be transmitted through dog bites and 99% could identify at least one clinical sign of canine rabies, awareness of the fatality of rabies in humans (43.1%) and dogs (26.3%) once symptoms appear was lower. Furthermore, only 69% would observe a biting dog for 10 days, and approximately 20.4% were familiar with proper dog-bite wound care. Only 20.6% knew that puppies could be vaccinated before three months. Among owners with vaccinated dogs, 78% found the cost (US $34 or less) acceptable. Regarding vaccination practices, 58% had their dogs vaccinated at home by veterinarians, and 86% reported that their veterinarians stored rabies vaccines on ice.

Overall, 53% of dog owners possessed sufficient rabies knowledge, 66% adopted adequate practices, and 17% exhibited positive attitudes. Multivariable logistic regression analyses indicated that sex, educational level, and length of dog ownership were not statistically associated with KAP scores.

While most dog owners demonstrated sufficient knowledge and appropriate practices, knowledge gaps persist, particularly regarding treatment, transmission, and control methods. Therefore, a targeted rabies awareness campaign is necessary to enhance dog owners' understanding of rabies prevention and control in Rwanda.

text:
Françoise Simon, an elderly widow, moves to the village of Les Laveuses on the Loire to open a small restaurant. Her business thrives locally until a notable food critic features it in a national magazine, bringing unwanted attention. Her nephew Yannick and his wife Laure arrive, hoping to capitalize on Françoise's newfound fame.

Françoise is not who she seems. Her real name is Framboise Dartigen, the sole surviving child of Mirabelle Dartigen, a woman despised for an event during World War II. Framboise, then nine, was deeply affected by these events and has hidden her true identity ever since.

Framboise's brother Cassis and sister Reine-Claude lost their father early in life. Their mother, Mirabelle, was a stern woman, more affectionate towards her fruit trees than her children. When the Germans occupied Les Laveuses, Mirabelle's toughness intensified. The children, unsupervised, befriended a young German soldier, Tomas, who initially won them over with black-market goods. Tomas manipulated them into providing information about their neighbors.

Framboise, closest to Tomas, blames herself for the chain of events leading to Tomas' death, the Gestapo's retaliation killing a dozen villagers, and Mirabelle's flight from their home. Sixty years later, Framboise relives these traumatic events, trying to understand their impact on her life.

As the truth surfaces, Framboise learns to confront those who threaten her, forgive herself and her mother, and reconnect with her two estranged daughters. She finally finds peace with her past.

 The story is written from the point of view of Françoise Simon, an elderly widow, who moves into the village of Les Laveuses on the Loire to open a small restaurant. Her business is moderately successful locally, until a notable food critic brings it to prominence in a national magazine. This brings undue attention to Françoise and her business, and brings a visit from her nephew Yannick and his grasping wife, Laure, both eager to profit from Françoise's sudden popularity. But Françoise Simon is not quite who she claims to be. Her real name is Framboise Dartigen, and she is the only surviving child of Mirabelle Dartigen, a woman still remembered and hated for an incident that happened when Framboise was nine, during the Second World War. Framboise has been profoundly marked by this incident and the events leading up to it, and still feels the need to hide who she is. The arrival of Luc and Laure threatens the new life she has built for herself, and forces her to confront the past. Framboise, her brother Cassis and her sister Reine-Claude lost their father early. Their mother, Mirabelle Dartigen, was a difficult woman, prone to crippling migraines and mre tender with her fruit trees than with her own children. Faced with having to bring up three children and run a farm alone, Mirabelle had to be very tough; sadly, this toughness translated into a lack of outward affection towards her children. When the war came and the Germans occupied Les Laveuses, Mirabelle had to be tougher than ever; the children, with no-one to supervise them, ran wild, eventually falling under the spell of a young German soldier, Tomas, who first bribed them with black-market goods like oranges or chocolate, then manipulated them into secretly giving him information about their friends and neighbours. Framboise, the youngest child, who was nine at the time, and whose relationship with her mother was especially tortuous, became closest to Tomas, and now blames herself for the series of events that resulted in Tomas' death, the retribution killing of a dozen villagers by the Gestapo and Mirabelle's flight from the family home. Now, sixty years later, Framboise relives these traumatic events and tries to understand how they have shaped her life and relationships. Eventually, as the truth emerges, she learns how to face down the bullies who threaten her, as well as to forgive herself and her mother, to give herself permission to love, to reconnect with her two estranged daughters and to finally put the past to rest.
</source>

text:
Researchers investigated neck proprioception in individuals with chronic non-specific low back pain (CNSLBP) and compared it to healthy controls. Previous studies suggest that CNSLBP patients exhibit poorer performance in postural tasks, yet neck proprioception remains unexplored in this population despite its critical role in posture and trunk alignment. This study aimed to fill that gap by comparing cervical joint reposition error between the two groups.

The study measured cervical joint reposition error five times in neutral head position, and at 30° and 60° left and right head rotations. The primary outcome was the mean cervical joint repositioning error of the head. Forty-six participants took part: 24 with CNSLBP (54 ± 16 years, 14 females) and 22 healthy controls (36 ± 13 years, 13 females).

Results revealed no statistically significant differences in mean cervical joint repositioning error between patients and controls across all tested positions. CNSLBP patients exhibited a deviation range of 1.57° to 3.27°, while healthy controls showed a range of 1.46° to 2.26°. Both groups demonstrated an overshooting tendency in the neutral head position.

The findings indicate that CNSLBP patients do not exhibit impaired head positioning accuracy. This suggests that sensorimotor control issues in CNSLBP may occur at other levels of the movement system. Future research should prioritize identifying the sources of these aberrations.

The ability to accurately position the head does not seem to be impaired in patients with CNSLBP. This may suggest that sensorimotor control is affected on other levels of the movement system and future research should focus on methods to identify the source of these aberrations.

text:
Ecuador's strong defensive display and two well-taken goals secured a 2-0 victory over Poland in their second Group A World Cup match.

The thousands of Polish supporters who made the trip to Gelsenkirchen's Veltins-Arena witnessed their team's struggle to mount effective attacking plays.

Ecuador, who lost their captain and defender Ivan Hurtado to injury in the 67th minute, scored once in each half to claim the win. The first goal came midway through the first half, and the second came with just ten minutes remaining.

The opening twenty minutes saw both teams tentative, failing to create any clear scoring opportunities. When the first chance did arrive, Ecuador made the most of it. A throw-in from the right was flicked on into the path of Carlos Tenario, who nodded the ball past Artur Boruc and into the far corner of the net.

While possession was fairly even in the first half, Poland dominated the second period as Ecuador retained their lead and looked to counterattack. However, Poland's passing was often wayward, leading to numerous turnovers in the final third.

Ecuador doubled their lead ten minutes from time. In a rare Polish defensive error, the ball was played through their backline, leaving two Ecuador players with a clear run at goal. Boruc, stranded, could do nothing to prevent the second goal.

Poland's attack only began to click in the final five minutes, with their efforts striking both the crossbar and the post of Christian Mora's goal.

Much of the credit for Ecuador's performance goes to their defensive unit, particularly Giovanny Espinoza and the injured Hurtado. Ecuador's coach, Luis Suarez, will be hoping Hurtado recovers in time for their next match against Costa Rica. Meanwhile, Poland must prepare to face a German side who won their opening World Cup game on Friday.

text:
This study evaluated the survival rates of patients with cervical cancer (CC) in Poland. Given that Polish medical societies' recommendations for CC management align closely with ESGO and international guidelines, and considering that the Polish CC treatment system and mortality rates—70% higher than the EU average—justify investigating deviations from these recommendations, this article examines current CC management in Poland and compares it with ASCO guidelines.

The study involved a retrospective, multicenter analysis of medical records from 1247 patients with CC who completed at least two years of follow-up after treatment.

While concurrent radiotherapy and chemotherapy serve as the standard treatment for FIGO IB to IVA CC patients in enhanced- and maximum-resource settings, our analysis revealed that the percentage of Polish women receiving chemotherapy was lower than in countries with lower total survival rates.

Among IA to IIA CC patients, treatment methods adhered to ASCO guidelines for high-standard care countries.

Our findings, alongside inconsistencies in the Polish cervical cancer screening program, may explain the poorer survival rates among Polish women with CC.

text: Frank and Joe Hardy rush to the Pocono Mountains to aid their father's friend, retired police captain Thomas Maguire. Strange occurrences have plagued the area: dogs and men vanish, eerie screams echo through the night, and locals whisper of vengeful ghosts. The only traces of the captain are a flashlight with the initials "T.M.," torn plaid fabric, and two recently fired shotgun shells. Undeterred by Chet's growing unease, Frank and Joe vow to find Maguire. Neighbors attribute the bloodcurdling cries to a vengeful witch, but the boys discover something far more unexpected. Jane Purdy, a 15-year-old student at Woodmont High School in California, often feels left out of social circles. She envies the more popular girls like 16-year-old Marcy Stokes, who have boyfriends and exude confidence. Jane dreams of having a boyfriend but feels she lacks the sophistication and charm of the popular girls.

One day, while babysitting, Jane meets Stan Crandall, a 16-year-old delivery boy for a pet-food store. She is immediately attracted to him, despite her belief that he won't be interested in her due to her lack of sophistication. Surprisingly, Stan calls her later and asks her out on a date. However, Jane's joy turns to disappointment when she learns that Stan had already promised to take Bitsy to a dance before he met Jane. Stan feels obligated to keep his date with Bitsy, even though he isn't attracted to her.

Throughout the story, Jane's relationship with Stan fluctuates. She constantly worries about her status with him, fearing she might scare him off. After one outing, Jane interprets Stan's quiet and detached behavior as a sign that he's tired of her. However, she later discovers that he was actually sick with appendicitis.

In the end, Stan reassures Jane that she is his girlfriend. He gives her his ID bracelet as a symbol of their commitment to each other.

text:
This systematic review aimed to examine the existing literature on women's experiences traveling for abortion, focusing on travel distance, cost, delays, and other barriers to accessing services. As abortion providers and access to care face increasing limitations worldwide, the need for travel to obtain abortion services has grown. However, no comprehensive review of this topic has been conducted previously. This mixed-methods review summarizes both qualitative and quantitative studies on the subject.

We conducted a systematic search using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Popline, and Google Scholar in July 2016, with an update in March 2017 (PROSPERO registration # CRD42016046007). Our inclusion criteria were original research studies describing women’s experiences traveling for abortion. Two reviewers independently screened articles, extracted data, and determined final inclusion for analysis. We assessed study quality using CASP, STROBE, and MMAT checklists.

Our review included 59 publications: 46 quantitative studies, 12 qualitative studies, and 1 mixed-methods study. Most studies were published in the last five years, primarily used data from the US, and considered travel as a secondary outcome. Quantitative studies often measured travel as road or straight-line distance to an abortion provider, with some incorporating additional factors like financial cost, childcare needs, and disclosure risks. Qualitative studies explored regional disparities in abortion access, the impact of travel on abortion method choice, and women’s reasons for travel. While study quality was generally high, many lacked details on participant recruitment or bias considerations.

To facilitate comparisons across studies, standardized measurements of travel and its associated burdens should be implemented. Further research is needed to better understand and accurately capture the various dimensions of the burden of travel for abortion services on women’s lives.

To systematically review the literature on women’s experiences traveling for abortion and assess how this concept has been explored and operationalized, with a focus on travel distance, cost, delays, and other barriers to receiving services.

Increasing limitations on abortion providers and access to care have increased the necessity of travel for abortion services around the world. No systematic examination of women’s experiences traveling for abortion has been conducted; this mixed-methods review provides a summary of the qualitative and quantitative literature on this topic.

A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Popline, and Google Scholar in July 2016 and updated in March 2017 (PROSPERO registration # CRD42016046007). We included original research studies that described women’s experiences traveling for abortion. Two reviewers independently performed article screening, data extraction and determination of final inclusion for analysis. Critical appraisal was conducted using CASP, STROBE, and MMAT checklists.

We included 59 publications: 46 quantitative studies, 12 qualitative studies, and 1 mixed-methods study. Most studies were published in the last five years, relied on data from the US, and discussed travel as a secondary outcome of interest. In quantitative studies, travel was primarily conceptualized and measured as road or straight-line distance to abortion provider, though some studies also incorporated measures of burdens related to travel, such as financial cost, childcare needs, and unwanted disclosure of their abortion status to others. Qualitative studies explored regional disparities in access to abortion care, with a focus on the burdens related to travel, the impact of travel on abortion method choice, and women’s reasons for travel. Studies generally were of high quality, though many studies lacked information on participant recruitment or consideration of potential biases.

Standardized measurements of travel, including burdens associated with travel and more nuanced considerations of travel costs, should be implemented in order to facilitate comparison across studies. More research is needed to explore and accurately capture different dimensions of the burden of travel for abortion services on women’s lives.

text: This study presents the discovery and description of four new Capsicum species inhabiting Andean tropical forests in South America. *Capsicum benoistii*, a newly described species (incertae sedis), is confined to a limited area in south-central Ecuador and shares morphological similarities with the more widely distributed *C. geminifolium*, which is found in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. *Capsicum piuranum*, a member of the Andean clade, is native to northern Peru's Piura Department and exhibits a close resemblance to *C. caballeroi* from the Bolivian yungas, while also maintaining a genetic proximity to *C. geminifolium* and *C. lycianthoides*. Meanwhile, *C. longifolium*, also part of the Andean clade, ranges from northern Peru (Amazonas, Cajamarca, and Piura Departments) to southern Ecuador's Zamora-Chinchipe Province, and is morphologically akin to *C. dimorphum*. Lastly, *Capsicum neei*, belonging to the Bolivian clade, is endemic to southeastern Bolivia's Chuquisaca and Santa Cruz Departments within the Boliviano-Tucumano Forest, and bears a strong resemblance to the Bolivian endemic *C. minutiflorum*. Comprehensive descriptions, illustrations, distributions, and conservation assessments are provided for all new species. Additionally, chromosome numbers are reported for *C. piuranum* and *C. longifolium*. The phylogenetic analysis confirms the placement of three new species within previously recognized clades in the Capsicum genus.

Four new species of Capsicum (Capsiceae, Solanaceae) from Andean tropical forests in South America are described. Capsicum benoistii Hunz. ex Barboza sp. nov. (incertae sedis) is endemic to a restricted area in south-central Ecuador and is most similar to the more widespread C. geminifolium (Dammer) Hunz. (Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru). Capsicum piuranum Barboza & S. Leiva sp. nov. (Andean clade) is found in northern Peru (Department Piura) and is morphologically most similar to C. caballeroi M. Nee of the Bolivian yungas (Departments Santa Cruz and Cochabamba) but closely related to C. geminifolium and C. lycianthoides Bitter. Capsicum longifolium Barboza & S. Leiva sp. nov. (Andean clade) occurs from northern Peru (Departments Amazonas, Cajamarca, and Piura) to southern Ecuador (Province Zamora-Chinchipe), and is morphologically most similar to C. dimorphum (Miers) Kuntze (Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru). Capsicum neei Barboza & X. Reyes sp. nov. (Bolivian clade) is endemic to southeastern Bolivia (Departments Chuquisaca and Santa Cruz) in the Boliviano-Tucumano Forest, is morphologically most similar to another Bolivian endemic species C. minutiflorum Rusby (Hunz.), and is closely related to C. caballeroi. Complete descriptions, illustrations, distributions and conservation assessments of all new species are given. Chromosome numbers for C. piuranum and C. longifolium are also provided. Three of the new species were included in a new phylogenetic analysis for Capsicum; their positions were strongly resolved within clades previously recognized in the genus.

The US government alleges that those arrested were members of a long-standing spy ring involving Russian agents who adopted civilian identities. All face charges of acting as unlawful agents for Russia, which could result in prison sentences of up to five years. Additionally, nine of the suspects are charged with money laundering, an offense that carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

According to the US government, the suspects underwent training by the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service to gather information about US military policies, particularly those related to nuclear weapons. They also sought intelligence on leadership within the CIA and the White House.

The FBI claims that to achieve these objectives, the suspects were directed to live as American citizens under false identities, with some posing as married couples. Notably, some suspects established connections with influential US citizens, including a scientist involved in nuclear weapons research and a New York financier with ties to US government officials.

Communication with Russian authorities allegedly employed various methods. These included unique wireless internet connections and images posted online containing hidden messages, as well as more conventional techniques like burying messages or exchanging bags between agents.

Names in quotes are cover names, while those without quotes are the real names of the alleged agents. Couples are listed together, while those living alone are listed separately. The locations mentioned are where the suspects were arrested.

text:
This study explores the socio-demographic determinants influencing women's autonomy in reproductive health decision-making across 27 sub-Saharan African nations. Utilizing pooled data from Demographic and Health Surveys conducted between 2010 and 2016, binary and multivariate logistic regression models were employed to examine the relationships between women's socio-demographic factors and their decision-making power regarding sexual and reproductive health.

Variability in decision-making capacity was observed, with the lowest proportion of women able to negotiate condom use during sexual intercourse in Mali (16.6%) and the highest in Namibia (93.4%). Similarly, the ability to refuse sexual intercourse ranged from 18.3% in Mali to 92.4% in Namibia. Overall, approximately 50% of women could ask their partners to use a condom, 60% could refuse sex, and 70% could make at least one reproductive health decision.

Findings indicated that women residing in rural areas (OR = 0.51, CI = 0.48–0.54), with no formal education (OR = 0.11, CI = 0.10–0.12), adhering to Islam (OR = 0.29, CI = 0.27–0.31), unemployed (OR = 0.53, CI = 0.51–0.56), and whose partners had no education (OR = 0.17, CI = 0.16–0.19) were less likely to make decisions about their reproductive health.

Residence, age, education level, religion, occupation, and partner's education were significantly associated with women's decision-making regarding sexual intercourse, condom use, and the reproductive health decision-making index. This research contributes valuable insights to the discourse on reproductive health autonomy in Africa. Policymakers should target these socio-demographic factors to enhance women's autonomy and empower them to manage their sexual and reproductive health effectively.

Women’s ability to make decisions regarding their reproductive health has important implications for their health and well-being. We studied the socio-demographic factors affecting reproductive health decision-making among women in 27 sub-Sahara African countries.

The study made use of pooled data from current Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) conducted from January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2016 in 27 countries in sub-Sahara African. Binary and multivariate logistic regression models were used to investigate the associations of women’s socio-demographic factors with decision-making regarding sexual reproductive health.

The proportion of women who can ask their partners to use a condom during sexual intercourse ranged from lowest in Mali (16.6%) to highest in Namibia (93.4%). Furthermore, the proportion of women who can refuse sex ranged from 18.3% in Mali to 92.4% in Namibia. Overall, approximately every five out of ten women can ask their partners to use a condom, six out ten women could refuse their partners sex and seven out of ten women could make at least 1 decision. Women from rural areas (OR = 0.51, CI = 0.48–0.54), those with no education (OR = 0.11, CI = 0.10–0.12), Muslim women (OR = 0.29, CI = 0.27–0.31), women not working (OR = 0.53, CI = 0.51–0.56) and women whose partners had no education (OR = 0.17, CI = 0.16–0.19) were less likely to make a decision on their reproductive health.

Residence, age, level of education, religion, occupation and partner’s education were found to be associated with women’s decision-making about sexual intercourse, condom use and reproductive health decision-making index. This study contributes to the discourse on reproductive health decision-making in Africa. Policies and intervention targeted at improving women’s autonomy and empowering them to take charge of their sexual and reproductive health issues should be focused on these factors.
</source>

text:
Born in 1850 in New Mexico to a Spanish mother and a Scotsman, Fey Cameron was orphaned young in the town that would bear her name, Santa Fe. She was taken in by neighbors who, though dutiful, remained emotionally detached. As a teenager, impetuous Fey seized the chance to flee with Terry Dillon, a wandering salesman of questionable character. They traveled the Santa Fe Trail, with Fey convincing herself their relationship was one of love. Terry, at least temporarily, seemed content. At Raton Pass, they enlisted Richens Lacey Wootton to perform their marriage.

They continued east, Terry selling his dubious remedies, and Fey using her skills to supplement their income. Upon reaching Leavenworth, Kansas, they scraped together enough funds for train fares to New York. Arriving in New York City with no prospects, they quickly depleted their modest savings on food and lodging. Terry soon abandoned Fey for what he hoped would be better opportunities.

Fey, however, proved resourceful. Discovering her pregnancy, she sought help at a local women's infirmary, exchanging labor for residence. After her daughter Lucita's birth, Fey set her sights on Simeon Tower, a New York tycoon, seeing him as her path to financial security. She captivated Simeon and won his affections. After arranging a discreet divorce for Fey, they married and found happiness together.

Over the years, they strove to expand their wealth and social standing. But 1877 marked their undoing. Simeon faced near-total financial ruin, and Terry Dillon resurfaced, causing chaos. He attempted to lure Fey back and blackmail Simeon, leading to tragedy. Left bankrupt and ostracized, Fey returned to New Mexico with an ailing Simeon, seeking solace in the simple life.

text:
Charlie, the narrator of the novel writing under the alias "Charlie," is an adolescent about to start high school. He's apprehensive about this new chapter, partly because it's his first year without Michael, his only good friend who took his own life a few months prior. Charlie feels adrift, unable to lean on his parents or siblings who never really got him. The only person he ever felt truly close to was his Aunt Helen, who died in a car accident on his seventh birthday.

Things start to change when Charlie befriends two seniors, Sam and her step-brother Patrick. Along with his English teacher Bill, they introduce him to new experiences. Charlie writes about these in letters to an anonymous friend, whom he overhears girls at school talk about fondly. He dives into situations he'd never imagined: parties, seeing and performing in "Rocky Horror Picture Show," and even his first date. He also falls for Sam, pouring his feelings into his letters. He briefly dates Mary Elizabeth, another friend, but his heart belongs to Sam.

Charlie's world expands as he learns about love and relationships. He witnesses Patrick's secret romance with Brad, the football team's closeted quarterback. He also sees his sister's relationship turn ugly when her boyfriend hits her. This hits close to home, reminding Charlie of his Aunt Helen's abuse.

By the story's end, Charlie grows tremendously. He learns to engage with life, no longer afraid. In a symbolic moment at summer's end, Patrick and Sam take him through a tunnel again, this time standing tall in the truck bed, a stark contrast to the fearful boy he once was. He's a wallflower no more.

text:
Patients with chronic non-specific low back pain (CNSLBP) may perform poorly in postural tasks compared to healthy individuals. While neck proprioception plays a crucial role in posture and trunk alignment relative to the head, it has not been studied in low back pain patients. This study aimed to compare neck proprioception between CNSLBP patients and healthy individuals.

Researchers measured cervical joint reposition error five times consecutively in neutral head position, and at 30° and 60° left and right head rotations. The primary outcome was the mean cervical joint repositioning error of the head.

The study included 46 participants: 24 with CNSLBP (54 ± 16 years, 14 females) and 22 healthy controls (36 ± 13 years, 13 females). Comparisons revealed no significant group differences in mean cervical joint repositioning error across all tested positions. CNSLBP patients exhibited deviations ranging from 1.57° to 3.27°, while healthy controls showed deviations from 1.46° to 2.26°. Both groups demonstrated an overshooting tendency in the neutral head position.

These findings suggest that CNSLBP patients do not exhibit impaired head positioning ability. This implies that sensorimotor control issues may occur at other levels of the movement system. Future research should explore methods to identify the source of these aberrations.

text:
Richard Collier, a 36-year-old screenwriter, is facing a grim reality: an inoperable brain tumor. After flipping a coin, he decides to spend his remaining days at the historic Hotel del Coronado. Most of the story unfolds through Richard's journal entries, which he diligently updates. He becomes captivated by a photograph of a renowned stage actress, Elise McKenna, who performed at the hotel in the 1890s. His research reveals that she never married, had a protective manager named William Fawcett Robinson, and allegedly had a brief affair with a mysterious man during a stay at the hotel in 1896.

As Richard delves deeper, he becomes convinced that it's his destiny to time travel and become that enigmatic figure. Through extensive research, he develops a method to mentally transport himself into the past. After persistent effort, he succeeds. Initially, he feels disoriented and fears being pulled back to the present, but these sensations fade. Unsure of what to say to Elise when they finally meet, he's taken aback when she asks, "Is it you?" Later, she explains that two psychics predicted she'd meet a mysterious man at that exact time and place.

Richard pursues a relationship with Elise, navigating the social norms of the era. Mysteriously, his daily headaches vanish, and he believes his memories of the future will eventually fade. However, Robinson, suspecting Richard's intentions, hires two men to abduct him and leave him in a shed while Elise departs on a train. Richard escapes and returns to the hotel, only to find Elise still there. They share a passionate night together. In the early hours, Richard leaves the room and encounters Robinson. After a brief scuffle, Richard rushes back inside, casually flipping a coin. Too late, he realizes it's a 1970s coin, and its sight sends him hurtling back to the present.

The story concludes with the revelation that Richard died soon after. A doctor dismisses his time-travel experience as the fantasy of a dying man, but Richard's brother, who publishes the journal, remains uncertain.

<source>
 Farmer Boy is based on the childhood of husband, Almanzo Wilder, who grew up in the 1860s near the town of Malone in upstate New York. The book covers one year in Almanzo's life, beginning just before his ninth birthday, and describes in detail the endless chores involved in running the Wilder family farm. Young as he is, Almanzo rises before 5 a.m. every day to milk several cows and feed stock. In the growing season, he plants and tends crops; in winter, he hauls logs, helps fill the ice house, trains a team of young oxen, and sometimes—when his father can spare him—goes to school. The novel includes stories of Almanzo's brother Royal and his sisters Eliza Jane and Alice. While Laura Ingalls grows up in a little house on the western prairie, Almanzo Wilder is living on a big farm in New York State, where he and his brother and sisters work at their chores from dawn to dinner most days-no matter what the weather. There is still time for fun, though, especially with the horses, which Almanzo loves more than anything.
</source>

text:
Bruce Drexel returns to Provence after discovering his lover and brother-in-law, Piers, has taken his own life. His wife, Sylvie, has been institutionalized for some time. While making funeral arrangements, Bruce visits Avignon with his friend Toby. Together, they reflect on Bruce's life with Piers and Sylvie. Bruce remembers vivid winter scenes from when the three were first in love and recalls a novel about them written by Robin Sutcliffe.

In the next chapter, "Macabru," Bruce, Piers, and Sylvie travel to Egypt. There, they meet Akkad, who introduces them to a Gnostic cult. Akkad takes them to Macabru in the desert to explain the group's rituals. This section also includes a lengthy journey on the Nile, which mirrors a later trip on the Rhone in Livia.

The third chapter, "Sutcliffe, or the Venetian Documents," introduces a new narrator, casting doubt on the truth of the previous events. Sutcliffe faces various misadventures in Venice and reflects on his failed marriage to Pia, Bruce's sister.

The section titled "Life with Toby" brings us back to Bruce and Toby in Avignon. They discuss a theory about the Knights Templar, tying back to the Gnostic theme. This section is interrupted by another text, "The Green Notebook," which shifts the focus back to Sutcliffe.

"Monsieur" was initially written in a green notebook, and "A Green Notebook" consists mostly of the rough notes that preceded the novel. This part becomes quite fragmented.

The final section, "Dinner at Quartilla's," introduces another author, Blanford, who is writing a book featuring Sutcliffe as a character. Blanford dines with his friend, the elderly Duchess Tu, who is actually deceased.

The novel concludes with an Envoi, listing the lineage of characters throughout the story but providing no final resolution.

His wife, Sylvie, has been in an institution for a while, and during his visit to Avignon with his friend Toby, Bruce tends to funeral arrangements and reflects on his past with Piers and Sylvie. He remembers vivid winter scenes from when the three were deeply in love and recalls a novel about them written by Robin Sutcliffe. The next chapter, "Macabru," tells of Bruce, Piers, and Sylvie's trip to Egypt, where they encounter Akkad, who introduces them to a Gnostic cult. Akkad leads them to a desert place called Macabru to explain the cult's rituals. This section includes a lengthy Nile journey, which echoes a later Rhine journey in the story. "Sutcliffe, or the Venetian Documents" shifts focus to a new narrator, casting doubt on whether the earlier events were real or fictional. Sutcliffe faces various troubles in Venice and reflects on his failed marriage to Pia, Bruce's sister. The section "Life with Toby" brings us back to Bruce and Toby in Avignon, discussing a theory about the Knights Templar tied to the Gnostic theme. This discussion is interrupted by another text, "The Green Notebook," which revisits Sutcliffe. Initially, the novel was written in a green notebook, and this section contains mostly unrevised notes that came before the novel, becoming quite fragmented. "Dinner at Quartilla's" is the final part of the novel, introducing another author, Blanford, who is writing a book featuring Sutcliffe as a character. He shares a meal with his friend, the elderly Duchess Tu, who is actually deceased. The novel concludes with an Envoi listing the lineage of characters throughout the story, but without a definitive conclusion.

text:
Rabies, a zoonotic viral disease affecting all warm-blooded animals, poses a significant public health risk in Rwanda. Although vaccinating dogs can prevent human rabies transmission, the country lacks comprehensive data on rabies epidemiology. This study sought to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding rabies and its control among dog owners in Kigali, Rwanda.

We conducted a cross-sectional survey using a structured questionnaire among 137 dog owners selected from nine administrative sites. Participants were chosen through a two-stage random sampling procedure. Data analysis involved frequency distributions, chi-square tests of association, and binary logistic regressions to identify key factors associated with the response variables.

The findings revealed that 99.5% of respondents recognized at least one rabies-susceptible host. However, only 22.4% knew that dogs could develop rabies, and 21.3% were aware that rabies could affect humans. Nearly 73.6% understood that human rabies could be transmitted through dog bites, and 99% could identify at least one clinical sign of canine rabies. Furthermore, 81.8% knew that regular dog vaccination helps prevent human rabies cases, and 43.1% and 26.3% were aware of the fatality of rabies in humans and dogs, respectively, once clinical symptoms appear. Only 69% would observe a dog for 10 days after it bit a person or animal, and approximately 20.4% knew how to properly clean dog-bite wounds. Additionally, 20.6% were aware that puppies could receive rabies vaccination before three months of age. Among owners with vaccinated dogs, 78% were satisfied with the vaccination cost (US $ ≤ 34). Of all respondents, 58% had their dogs vaccinated at home by veterinarians, and 86% reported that their veterinarians stored rabies vaccines on ice in a cool box. Overall, 53% of dog owners had sufficient rabies knowledge, while 66% and 17% demonstrated adequate practices and positive attitudes toward rabies, respectively. Multivariable logistic regression analyses showed that sex, educational level, and length of dog ownership were not statistically associated with rabies KAP.

This study indicated that most dog owners possessed adequate rabies knowledge and practiced appropriate rabies control measures. However, knowledge gaps persist, particularly regarding treatment, transmission, and control methods. To address these gaps, a targeted rabies awareness campaign is recommended to enhance dog owners' understanding of rabies prevention and control in Rwanda.

Rabies is a public health threat in Rwanda, but the country does not have information on the epidemiology of rabies. A two-stage random sampling procedure was used to select the participants. Frequency distributions analysis and a series of chi-square tests of associations as well as binary logistic regressions were performed to determine the important factors associated with the response variables.

The results showed that 99.5% of respondents knew at least a host susceptible to rabies. Only 22.4% and 21.3% knew that dogs and people can develop rabies, respectively. Nearly 73.6% knew that human rabies can be transmitted through dog-bites and 99% could identify at least a clinical sign of canine rabies. Overall, 81.8% knew that regular vaccination of dogs helps to prevent dog-transmitted human rabies and 43.1% and 26.3% were aware that rabies in humans and in dogs are fatal once clinical symptoms have shown, respectively. Only 69% would observe a dog for 10 days after it bites a man or an animal. Approximately 20.4% were familiar with appropriate cleaning of dog-bites wounds, and 20.6% knew that puppies could receive rabies vaccination before they are three months old. Of those who owned vaccinated dogs, 78% were happy about the cost (US $ ≤ 34) of rabies vaccination. Of all the respondents, 58% had their dogs vaccinated at home by veterinarians while 86% indicated their veterinarians kept rabies vaccines on ice in a cool box. Overall, 53% of the dog owners had sufficient knowledge of rabies, whilst 66% and 17% adopted adequate practices and positive attitudes towards rabies, respectively. Multivariable logistic regression analyses indicated that none of the respondents’ sex, educational level, and the length of dog ownership were statistically associated with their knowledge, attitudes and practices of rabies.

This study showed that majority of the dog owners had sufficient knowledge and adopted appropriate practices of rabies. However there exist some knowledge gaps among the dog owners particularly on treatment, transmission and control methods. Therefore, rabies awareness campaign is required to upgrade rabies knowledge of the dog owners on rabies prevention and control in Rwanda.

text:
Egypt's economic challenges have intensified following a second currency rating downgrade by Standard & Poor's in four months. The downgrade, attributed to the country's dwindling foreign reserves and political uncertainty, comes as Egypt grapples with significant economic hurdles.

Egypt's foreign reserves have diminished by over 50 percent in the past year, now standing at approximately US$16 billion. To mitigate this shortfall and avert potential currency devaluation, Egypt has sought US$3.2 billion from the International Monetary Fund. However, this process could span several months.

Egypt's struggle to attract foreign investment and tourists, crucial for reserve replenishment, has already triggered a 1 percent depreciation of the Egyptian pound. Failure to address this foreign currency deficit may lead to further devaluation within the next two to three months.

Long-term recovery hinges on revitalizing tourism and foreign investments, both of which are currently hampered by ongoing unrest.

Egypt's tourism sector has been severely impacted. In 2010, tourism generated US$12.5 billion, but this figure plummeted by 30 percent to US$8.8 billion in 2011. Tourism contributes 11.6 percent to Egypt's GDP.

The Egyptian Revolution, which commenced on January 25, 2011, and resulted in President Hosni Mubarak's resignation on February 11, has been followed by sustained protests and instability. This turmoil has deterred potential visitors. Recently, 79 people were killed during a soccer event in Port Said, further tarnishing Egypt's image.

Last week, two U.S. female tourists and their Egyptian guide were kidnapped in the Sinai peninsula by Bedouin tribesmen but were released shortly afterward. The incident occurred in broad daylight on a busy road, following a visit to St. Catherine's Monastery. Masked tribesmen halted their bus, abducted the tourists at gunpoint, and fled into the mountains. Three other tourists were left on the bus. Local authorities conducted a search and negotiated with the Bedouin, who demanded the release of recently detained tribesmen. The U.S. hostages were released unharmed.

Egypt's tourism appeal lies in its ancient pyramids, the Nile River, Biblical sites like Mount Sinai, museums, and Red Sea coastal resorts. However, tourist numbers have dropped from 15 million in the previous year to 9 million, a 40 percent decrease.

Foreign investment is also lacking due to perceived instability. Mulyani Indrawati, managing director of the World Bank, noted that investors are reluctant to re-enter Arab Spring countries' markets until stability is restored. This situation is compounded by the fragile state of the regional and international economy.
