Standard & Poor's downgraded Egypt's currency rating for the second time in four months based on the country's shorfall in foreign reserves and shaky political transition. It's the latest development for a nation facing mounting economic diffuclties.

Egypt's foreign reserves fell by over 50 percent last year to about US$16 billion. Egypt has requested US$3.2 billion from the International Monetary Fund to bolster its reserves and prevent a devalation but that could take months.

Experts say that Egypt's problem of attracting foreign investment and tourists, which are two sources that would increase reserves, has already caused the Egyptian pound to lose 1 percent of its value and if the country doesn't solve the shortfall in foriegn currency, it could even lead to a further currency devaluation within the next two to three months.

The long-term solution is to restore tourism and foreign investments but both are suffering because of the continuing unrest.

Egyptian tourism suffered this past year as a result of a revolution, a transition to an elected government, and continuing signs of unrest and instability.

The Egyptian Revolution began on January 25 last year and President Hosni Mubarak resigned over two weeks later on February 11. The protests have continued as Egyptians grew uncomfortable with the military's control over the transition. At the start of this month, 79 people were killed at a soccer event in Port Said.

Tourism in Egypt accounted for US$12.5 billion in 2010 but fell 30 percent, or US$8.8 billion, in 2011, according to Mounir Fakhry Abdel Nour, Egypt's tourism minister. Tourism accounts for 11.6 percent of Egypt's GDP.

Last week, two U.S. female tourists and their Egyptian guide were abducted in the Sinai peninsula by Bedouin tribesmen and released shortly afterward.

The kidnapping took place in broad daylight on a busy road while the tourists travelled after a visit to St. Catherine's Monastery. Masked tribesmen stopped their bus, abducted the tourists by gunpoint, and escaped into the mountains. Three other tourists of unknown nationalities were left on the bus. Local authorities organized a search which ended in negotiations with local Bedouin tribesmen. text:
This study sought to appraise the quality and evidence base of motor learning research on contextual interference (CI) effects—comparing blocked and random practice orders—in children with brain lesions and typically developing (TD) children. Eight databases were systematically searched using predefined terms. Controlled studies examining CI effects in these populations were included. Two authors independently assessed evidence level, conduct quality, and risk of bias. A best evidence synthesis was conducted.

Twenty-five studies on TD children were included, one of which also evaluated children with cerebral palsy. Evidence levels ranged from I to III. Conduct quality was generally low, and risk of bias was high, primarily due to methodological flaws or inadequate reporting. Best evidence synthesis revealed predominantly no or conflicting evidence, with single tasks showing limited to moderate evidence supporting CI effects in TD children.

There is a marked paucity of high-quality evidence regarding CI effects in children practicing multiple tasks within a session, particularly those with brain lesions.

We aimed to identify and evaluate the quality and evidence of the motor learning literature about intervention studies regarding the contextual interference (CI) effect (blocked vs. random practice order) in children with brain lesions and typically developing (TD) children.

There is a severe limitation of good-quality evidence about the CI effect in children who practice different tasks in one session, especially in children with brain lesions.

text:
Ecuador secured a 3-0 win over Costa Rica in their World Cup match at the AOL Arena in Hamburg on Thursday. This victory ensured that both Ecuador and Germany, each with six points from two games, advanced from Group A into the knockout phase of the tournament.

The match was relatively straightforward for Ecuador's Colombian coach, Luis Suarez. He had the luxury of resting three key players—goal scorer Carlos Tenorio, playmaker Luis Valencia, and center-back Giovanny Espinoza—by substituting them out before the game concluded.

Ecuador maintained possession well and controlled the tempo of the game. Meanwhile, Costa Rica, under coach Alexandre Guimaraes, struggled to increase the pace and apply sustained pressure on Ecuador's goalkeeper, Christian Mora.

Ecuador took the lead early, with Valencia delivering a cross from the right side of the penalty area. Tenorio, unmarked in front of Costa Rican goalkeeper Jose Porras, headed the ball into the net just seven minutes into the game.

Both teams had chances to score before halftime. Douglas Sequeira was unmarked at the Ecuador far post but missed his header. Ecuador's Edison Mendez and Agustin Delgado nearly scored a similar goal, but Delgado's shot skewed wide. Delgado later scored with a hard shot from an angle inside the penalty area, beating Porras to his near post.

Tenorio's substitute, Kaviedes, also had a mixed sequence of chances. After a save from Porras and a missed header, Kaviedes finally connected with a beautiful far-post volley, finishing off another Mendez cross.

Costa Rica had a stroke of bad luck when Alvaro Saborio's clever chip beat Mora but hit the post. However, Costa Rica did not create as many clear scoring opportunities as Ecuador. Long shots from Carlos Hernandez and Mauricio Solis were notable but insufficient against a solid Ecuador defense, which secured its second consecutive World Cup clean sheet. Ecuador will now face Germany on June 20 to determine the winner of Group A.

High-frequency sound (HSS) technology operates on a simple yet fascinating principle. Sounds with frequencies too high for human ears to detect don't spread out like normal sound waves. This allows them to be directed precisely at specific individuals. The targeted person hears a sound seeming to come from within, while others nearby hear nothing. This could revolutionize public spaces by reducing noise pollution. Imagine announcements, instructions, or even advertisements directed at you alone, without disturbing others. In the same room, people could enjoy different music without headphones. Boost the volume, and HSS could aid military or law enforcement. HSS beams can be focused up to 500 yards, transmitting warnings or temporarily stunning and disabling individuals with non-lethal force.

Meanwhile, a novel mode of personal transportation is taking flight. The AirScooter™, a helicopter-like vehicle, is set to hit the market later this year with an estimated price tag under $50,000. Weighing less than 300 pounds and capable of carrying an additional 350 pounds, the AirScooter runs on standard gasoline, not expensive aviation fuel. With a 5-gallon tank, it can travel for about 2 hours at 55 m.p.h., reaching altitudes up to 10,000 feet. Its ultralight design means no pilot license is required for operation. The AirScooter's light weight is achieved through a new AeroTwin 4-stroke engine, designed by motorcycle racing engine specialists at Pearson Motor Co. in New Zealand. This engine features two rotors on a single shaft, spinning in opposite directions, eliminating the need for a tail rotor. Steering is intuitive, using a motorcycle-like handlebar. Throttle control adjusts altitude, turning the bars rotates the craft, and moving them like a joystick steers in various directions, including reverse. For a closer look, pictures and videos are available on the AirScooter.com website.

Behind this innovation is independent inventor Glenn Norris, a self-educated man with a boundless curiosity. Despite not completing third grade in traditional schooling, Norris has been developing inventions for over 30 years, with a focus on audio technology since he was eight. At 63, he's a father of 11. Norris plans to use any prize money to establish a foundation supporting struggling, independent inventors like himself.

text:
Four new species of Capsicum (Capsiceae, Solanaceae) from Andean tropical forests in South America are described here. Capsicum benoistii Hunz. ex Barboza, a species whose phylogenetic placement is uncertain, is endemic to a restricted area in south-central Ecuador. It is most similar to the more widespread C. geminifolium (Dammer) Hunz., which is found in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. Capsicum piuranum Barboza & S. Leiva, belonging to the Andean clade, occurs in northern Peru (Department Piura). Morphologically, it resembles C. caballeroi M. Nee of the Bolivian yungas (Departments Santa Cruz and Cochabamba), but is closely related to both C. geminifolium and C. lycianthoides Bitter. Capsicum longifolium Barboza & S. Leiva, also part of the Andean clade, ranges from northern Peru (Departments Amazonas, Cajamarca, and Piura) to southern Ecuador (Province Zamora-Chinchipe). It is morphologically similar to C. dimorphum (Miers) Kuntze, distributed across Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. Capsicum neei Barboza & X. Reyes, a member of the Bolivian clade, is endemic to southeastern Bolivia (Departments Chuquisaca and Santa Cruz) in the Boliviano-Tucumano Forest. It closely resembles the Bolivian endemic species C. minutiflorum Rusby (Hunz.) and is closely related to C. caballeroi.

Complete descriptions, illustrations, distributions, and conservation assessments are provided for all new species. Chromosome numbers are also reported for C. piuranum and C. longifolium. Three of the new species were included in a phylogenetic analysis of Capsicum; their positions were strongly resolved within clades previously recognized in the genus.

text: African populations exhibit a remarkable degree of genetic diversity, potentially driven by natural selection pressures. This diversity has been linked to variations in susceptibility to infectious diseases, notably malaria. Given this association, it is crucial to account for genetic diversity when evaluating clinical trial outcomes in malaria-endemic regions. This study sought to investigate erythrocyte trait polymorphisms across diverse populations in malaria-endemic areas of Mali. Cross-sectional surveys were conducted among various ethnic groups residing in these areas. Following informed consent, 6 milliliters of whole blood were collected from each participant for analysis. Phenotyping of ABO, Rh, Kell, MNSs, Kidd, and Duffy blood group systems was performed using gel filtration techniques. The study included 231 individuals from six villages. The most prevalent blood group phenotypes were O (40.7%) and A (31.2%), with corresponding allele frequencies of 0.65 and 0.21. Washington Governor Christine Gregoire declared a state of emergency on Sunday, as more reports of storm-related casualties came in. The state's National Guard has been called in to help distribute supplies.

Thousands were still without power in the coastal and Puget Sound areas, though most urban spots had their electricity back by Sunday afternoon. Outages were mostly in rural and unincorporated zones. Puget Sound Energy reported that around 500,000 of the 700,000 customers who lost power were back online by Sunday evening. Seattle City Light, the city's independent utility, said only 18,000 customers were still without power by Monday morning, down from a high of 175,000.

Four more deaths related to the post-storm power outage were reported by Monday, bringing the total to eight. In Gig Harbor, a man was electrocuted by a downed power line while walking his dog. Another man in Spanaway died when an unattended candle started a house fire.

On Monday, four new carbon monoxide deaths were reported in a family of five in Burien due to an indoor generator. In Canada, which also saw some damage from the week's storms, two carbon monoxide deaths were reported in southern British Columbia. Despite ongoing warnings, hospitals are still treating cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, like a family in Shoreline, Washington who went to the hospital after reporting symptoms from their indoor grill. Neighbors of the Burien family suggested that noise concerns might be leading people to place noisy generators indoors.

The Red Cross set up shelters in King and other affected counties for those without power or food. Hotels were fully booked as families sought shelter, especially in Seattle. Restaurants saw a rush of business as people looked for a hot meal. Tons of perishable food were expected to have gone bad after the prolonged outage disabled refrigerators and freezers in homes and stores.

Many without power stayed with friends or family who still had electricity, while others traveled to unaffected areas. The widespread outage made long-distance travel risky on some major routes, with roadway lighting, cellular towers, and services out of order.

Most major roadways closed during the storm were reopened on Friday. The 520 Floating Bridge over Lake Washington, a key route to the Eastside, had minor damage. Amtrak, which had suspended its Cascades service, started up again on Saturday evening. Sea-Tac Airport resumed operations with fewer flights after a brief power outage on Friday knocked out the airport's radar, grounding all planes until it was fixed.

text:
Ecuador secured a 3-0 victory over Costa Rica at the AOL Arena in Hamburg on Thursday, creating numerous chances and keeping their opponents largely quiet.

This win for the South American team meant that both Ecuador and Germany, each with six points from two games, advanced from Group A into the knockout phase of the FIFA World Cup in Germany.

The match was comfortable for Ecuador's Colombian coach Luis Suárez. He chose to rest three key players—goal scorer Carlos Tenorio, playmaker Luis Valencia, and impressive center-back Giovanny Espinoza—by bringing on substitutes before the game ended.

Ecuador maintained possession well and controlled the tempo of the game. Meanwhile, Alexandre Guimarães's team did not appear capable of increasing the pace or sustaining pressure on Christian Mora's goal.

The first goal came after just seven minutes. Valencia, positioned to the right of the penalty area, crossed the ball. Tenorio, unmarked in front of Jose Porras, dove to head it in.

Both teams missed chances before halftime. Douglas Sequeira, unmarked at the far post, mistimed his header, sending it wide. Later, Edison Méndez and Agustín Delgado nearly replicated the first goal, but Delgado's shot was weak and went wide.

After another shot was saved, Delgado finally scored with his third attempt. He struck the ball hard from an angle inside the penalty area, beating Porras on his near post.

Then, Tenorio's substitute Iván Kaviedes had his turn. First, Porras made a save, then Kaviedes headed wide. Finally, he connected with a beautiful far-post volley, finishing off another Méndez cross.

Costa Rica had a stroke of bad luck when Álvaro Saborio's clever first-time chip beat Mora but hit the post. However, they had not created as many clear chances as Ecuador had at the other end.

Long shots from Carlos Hernández and Mauricio Solís were notable but were acts of individual play, not a sign of a coordinated attack. Ecuador's defense held firm, securing its second consecutive World Cup shutout. The team will now play Germany on June 20 to determine the winner of Group A.

High-frequency sound (HSS) technology operates on a unique principle: sounds with frequencies above human hearing range do not disperse like typical audible waves. text:
Françoise Simon, an elderly widow, moves to the village of Les Laveuses on the Loire to open a small restaurant. Her business thrives locally until a notable food critic features it in a national magazine, bringing unwanted attention. This sudden fame attracts her nephew Yannick and his wife Laure, both hoping to capitalize on Françoise's newfound popularity.

Françoise is not who she appears to be. Her real name is Framboise Dartigen, the sole surviving child of Mirabelle Dartigen. Mirabelle is still remembered and reviled for an incident during the Second World War when Framboise was nine. This event and its aftermath have deeply affected Framboise, compelling her to hide her true identity. The arrival of Yannick and Laure disrupts the life she has built and forces her to confront her past.

Framboise, her brother Cassis, and her sister Reine-Claude lost their father early in life. Their mother, Mirabelle, was a hard woman, often incapacitated by migraines and more affectionate with her fruit trees than her children. Raising three children and managing a farm alone required immense toughness, which Mirabelle directed outward rather than toward her family. When the Germans occupied Les Laveuses, Mirabelle had to be even tougher. The children, left unsupervised, ran wild and fell under the influence of a young German soldier, Tomas. He initially bribed them with black-market goods like oranges and chocolate, then manipulated them into providing information about their friends and neighbors.

Framboise, the youngest, became closest to Tomas and blames herself for the events leading to his death. In retaliation, the Gestapo killed a dozen villagers and Mirabelle fled the family home. Sixty years later, Framboise relives these traumatic events, trying to understand their impact on her life and relationships.

As the truth emerges, she learns to stand up to those who threaten her, forgive herself and her mother, and allow herself to love. She reconnects with her two estranged daughters and finally lays the past to rest.

text:
Women's autonomy in reproductive health decision-making significantly influences their health and well-being. This study examined the socio-demographic factors affecting reproductive health decision-making among women in 27 sub-Saharan African countries.

Utilizing pooled data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) conducted between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2016, we employed binary and multivariate logistic regression models to investigate the associations between women's socio-demographic factors and sexual reproductive health decision-making.

The proportion of women who could request condom use during sexual intercourse varied markedly, from a low of 16.6% in Mali to a high of 93.4% in Namibia. Similarly, the proportion of women who could refuse sex ranged from 18.3% in Mali to 92.4% in Namibia. Overall, approximately 50% of women could ask their partners to use a condom, 60% could refuse sex, and 70% could make at least one reproductive health decision.

Our analysis revealed that women from rural areas (OR = 0.51, CI = 0.48–0.54), those with no education (OR = 0.11, CI = 0.10–0.12), Muslim women (OR = 0.29, CI = 0.27–0.31), unemployed women (OR = 0.53, CI = 0.51–0.56), and women whose partners had no education (OR = 0.17, CI = 0.16–0.19) were less likely to make decisions about their reproductive health.

Residence, age, education level, religion, occupation, and partner's education were significantly associated with women's decision-making regarding sexual intercourse, condom use, and the reproductive health decision-making index. This study contributes valuable insights to the discourse on reproductive health decision-making in Africa. Policies and interventions aimed at enhancing women's autonomy and empowering them to manage their sexual and reproductive health should focus on these identified factors.

When dogs and men abruptly vanish, and eerie screams echo through the night, tales of vengeful ghosts seem almost plausible. These strange events draw Frank and Joe Hardy to the Pocono Mountains. They aim to assist their father's friend, retired police captain Thomas Maguire, in solving the mystery of Black Hollow.

Upon arriving at Maguire's cabin, the boys find it empty. In the surrounding woods, they discover sparse clues: a flashlight bearing the initials "T.M.," shreds of bright plaid cloth, and two recently fired shotgun shells. Despite Chet Morton's apprehension after a night filled with unsettling screams, Frank and Joe remain resolved to find the captain.

Neighbors attribute the bloodcurdling cries to a legendary witch haunting Black Hollow, seeking revenge. However, it is an unlikely ally—a small puppy—that aids the boys in uncovering an unusual and surprising sequence of events. This involves a mute boy, an elusive hermit, and a daring puma trainer.

text:
Born in the small town of Middleton, Buster Casey was no ordinary kid. He hit the ground running with a superpowered sense of smell and taste that put everyone else to shame. But it was a childhood prank gone wrong that really sealed his fate. You see, young Buster had a thing for animal organs, and his little stunt left a lot of people feeling, well, green around the gills. As they lost their lunches, they made a sound that went something like "rant," and just like that, our boy got his nickname.

But Buster, or Rant as we now know him, was just getting started. He stumbled upon a pile of cash that would've made Scrooge McDuck blush, turning Middleton's economy upside down. Then, in a twist that even the most creative minds couldn't have predicted, Rant became obsessed with getting chomped by rabid critters and venomous vipers. Turns out, a little black widow love bite had a, well, stimulating effect on our friend. He used this newfound "talent" to cut class, bully his way to an early diploma, and pocket a nice chunk of change to boot.

Rant packed his bags and headed for the city, where he discovered that the world had taken a turn for the dystopian. The urban jungle was split into two classes: the Daytimers, who had it made, and the Nighttimers, who were left to fend for themselves after the sun went down. Rant joined the Nighttimer ranks and dove headfirst into their underground scene, where the main attraction was "Party Crashing" - a high-speed, high-stakes demolition derby played out on the city streets.

Picture this: a bunch of cars, each sporting a silly flag like a Christmas tree or "Just Married" sign, cruising around at night, trying to crash into each other - but not too hard, mind you. It was all organized by some shadowy figure, and Rant was hooked. That's where he met Echo Lawrence, his fellow crasher and the love of his life.

But Rant's antics didn't stop there. He kicked off a nationwide rabies epidemic that quickly spiraled out of control, turning into something straight out of a zombie apocalypse movie. The infected? Shot on sight, no questions asked.

Rant's reign of chaos came to a screeching halt during a Party Crashing event, broadcast live on national TV and radio. Millions tuned in to watch - or rather, listen - as Rant met his supposed demise. But here's the kicker: when they pried open the car, Rant's body was nowhere to be found.

In the aftermath, people had a lot to say about Rant's mysterious disappearance and what it all meant. Some speculated that crashing a car in a certain state of mind could knock you right out of time, letting you go back and off your ancestors - basically becoming immortal. Others thought that, well, incest could turn you into something more than human. Sound familiar? That's right, they were talking about Green Taylor Simms, another Party Crasher with some seriously shady ties to our main man, Rant.

Standard & Poor's downgraded Egypt's currency rating for the second time in four months, citing the country's decline in foreign reserves and uncertain political transition. This development follows mounting economic challenges faced by the nation.

Egypt's foreign reserves dropped by over 50 percent last year, reaching approximately $16 billion. The country has requested $3.2 billion from the International Monetary Fund to strengthen its reserves and avoid devaluation, but this process could take months.

Experts note that Egypt's struggle to attract foreign investment and tourists—key sources for increasing reserves—has already caused the Egyptian pound to lose 1 percent of its value. Without addressing the foreign currency shortfall, a further devaluation could occur within the next two to three months.

The long-term solution involves restoring tourism and foreign investments. However, both sectors suffer due to ongoing unrest.

Egyptian tourism declined significantly over the past year due to revolution, political transition, and persistent instability. The Egyptian Revolution began on January 25, leading to President Hosni Mubarak's resignation on February 11. Protests have continued as Egyptians express discomfort with the military's control over the transition. In early March, 79 people were killed during a soccer event in Port Said.

Tourism contributed $12.5 billion to Egypt's economy in 2010 but fell by 30 percent, to $8.8 billion, in 2011, according to Mounir Fakhry Abdel Nour, Egypt's tourism minister. Tourism accounts for 11.6 percent of Egypt's GDP.

Last week, two U.S. female tourists and their Egyptian guide were abducted in the Sinai peninsula by Bedouin tribesmen and released shortly afterward. The kidnapping occurred in broad daylight on a busy road as the tourists traveled after visiting St. Catherine's Monastery. Masked tribesmen stopped their bus, abducted the tourists at gunpoint, and fled into the mountains. Three other tourists of unknown nationalities were left on the bus. Local authorities conducted a search, which ended in negotiations with local Bedouin tribesmen. The Bedouin demanded the release of recently apprehended tribesmen, who had been detained for drug trafficking and robbery. The U.S. hostages were released unharmed, Abdel Nour reported.

Egypt offers ancient pyramids, the Nile River, Biblical sites like Mount Sinai, museums, and Red Sea coastal resorts. However, the number of tourists plummeted from 15 million to 9 million last year, a 40 percent drop.

Egypt's investment climate also faces significant challenges due to perceptions of instability. Mulyani Indrawati, managing director of the World Bank, stated that investors are hesitant to re-enter Arab Spring countries' markets until stability is restored. This situation has been compounded by the precarious state of the regional and international economy.

text:
Fey Cameron entered the world in 1850 in New Mexico, born to a Spanish mother and a Scotsman. Orphaned young, she was taken in by indifferent neighbors in Santa Fe, the town that shared her name. As a teenager, Fey's fiery spirit led her to join Terry Dillon, a slippery traveling salesman, and they set off together along the Santa Fe Trail. Fey convinced herself that they were in love, and Terry, at least for the moment, was not unpleasant.

At Raton Pass, Terry enlisted Richens Lacey Wootton to marry them. They journeyed east, Terry selling his dubious medicines, and Fey using her various talents to supplement their income. When they reached Leavenworth, Kansas, they had saved enough for train fares to New York. Upon arriving in the city, however, they found no prospects waiting for them. Their small savings quickly dwindled on food and board, and Terry soon abandoned Fey.

Fey discovered she was pregnant and sought help at a local women's infirmary. In exchange for assisting with the work, she was allowed to live there. After her daughter Lucita was born, Fey set her sights on Simeon Tower, a New York tycoon, seeing him as her ticket to financial security. She won his heart, and after securing a discreet divorce, they married and found happiness together.

Over the years, Fey and Simeon worked to expand their fortune and social standing. But in 1877, their world began to crumble. Simeon faced near-total financial ruin, and Terry Dillon resurfaced, attempting to lure Fey back and blackmail Simeon. The ensuing tragedy left them bankrupt and shunned by society. Fey eventually took ailing Simeon back to the simple life in New Mexico, where they spent their remaining days.

text:
There's a lack of data comparing body composition changes, adipokines, and inflammatory markers after initial therapy with nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (N(t)RTI)-sparing or containing regimens.

This body composition sub-study is part of NEAT 001/ANRS 143, a randomized trial that compared darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) plus either raltegravir (RAL) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) in 805 antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naïve HIV-infected adults. The main goal was to see how limb fat percentage changed at week 96. Secondary goals included looking at how these changes related to metabolic markers like IL-6, insulin, leptin, adiponectin, and FGF-23.

In this study, 126 subjects (61 on DRV/r + RAL and 65 on DRV/r + TDF/FTC) were included. The rate of BMI change between the groups for RAL versus TDF/FTC at week 96 was 1.5% per 48-week period (p = 0.015). The rate of change in limb fat mass, trunk fat mass, total body fat, and total lean mass for RAL versus TDF/FTC at week 96 was 2.5% (p = 0.38), 7.3% (p = 0.021), 4.9% (p = 0.061), and 1.3% (p = 0.12) respectively.

 Baseline insulin and leptin levels were linked to baseline limb fat and trunk fat mass [r = 0.31 (p = 0.0043)/r = 0.28 (p = 0.0011) for limb fat, and r = 0.63 (p<0.0001)/r = 0.50(p<0.0001) for trunk fat]. After adjusting for other factors, a 10% faster increase in leptin between baseline and week 48 was tied to a quicker increase in limb fat at week 48 (0.5% per 48 weeks, p<0.001), total body fat mass (0.6% per 48 weeks, p<0.001), and trunk fat mass (0.3% per 48 weeks, p = 0.0026).

After week 96, a N(t)RTI-sparing regimen of DRV/r + RAL led to a greater percentage increase in body composition variables, with only changes in trunk fat mass and BMI being significant.

text: Neuroangiostrongyliasis, caused by Angiostrongylus cantonensis, has been documented in Hawaiʻi since the 1950s, with a recent increase in cases, particularly on East Hawaiʻi Island. This rise is linked to the introduction of the semi-slug Parmarion martensi. In areas lacking water infrastructure, households rely on rainwater catchment systems, which are not regulated by federal, state, or county authorities. Despite evidence suggesting that slugs and snails can contaminate water and transmit infection, this potential route has not been addressed by regulatory bodies. This study investigates several key aspects: the emergence of live, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae from drowned, non-native gastropods; the distribution of larvae in undisturbed water; the longevity of free-living larvae in water; and the effectiveness of rainwater catchment filters in blocking infective-stage larvae. Larvae were recovered from minced and whole gastropods drowned in municipal water or rainwater, with approximately 94% collected from the water column's bottom 72–96 hours post-drowning. Infective-stage larvae remained active for 21 days in municipal water. Histological analysis of P. martensi revealed nematode larvae near the gastropod's body wall, suggesting potential larval shedding in slime. Tissue squashes proved effective for quick screening. Notably, live, infective-stage larvae passed through polypropylene sediment filters with ratings of 20 μm, 10 μm, 5 μm, and 1 μm, but were blocked by a 5 μm carbon block filter. These findings indicate that live, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae can emerge from drowned snails and slugs, survive in water for prolonged periods, and potentially enter household water supplies. This study underscores the urgent need to investigate and understand the role of contaminated water in transmitting neuroangiostrongyliasis.

<source>
Neuroangiostrongyliasis, caused by Angiostrongylus cantonensis, has been reported in Hawaiʻi since the 1950's. An increase in cases is being reported primarily from East Hawaiʻi Island, correlated with the introduction of the semi-slug Parmarion martensi. Households in areas lacking infrastructure for water must use rainwater catchment as their primary domestic water supply, for which there is no federal, state, or county regulation. Despite evidence that slugs and snails can contaminate water and cause infection, regulatory bodies have not addressed this potential transmission route. This study evaluates: 1) the emergence of live, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae from drowned, non-native, pestiforous gastropods; 2) larvae location in an undisturbed water column; 3) longevity of free-living larvae in water; and 4) effectiveness of rainwater catchment filters in blocking infective-stage larvae. Larvae were shed from minced and whole gastropods drowned in either municipal water or rainwater with ~94% of larvae recovered from the bottom of the water column 72–96 hours post drowning. Infective-stage larvae were active for 21 days in municipal water. Histological sectioning of P. martensi showed proximity of nematode larvae to the body wall of the gastropod, consistent with the potential for shedding of larvae in slime. Gastropod tissue squashes showed effectivity as a quick screening method. Live, infective-stage larvae were able to traverse rainwater catchment polypropylene sediment filters of 20 μm, 10 μm, 5 μm, and 1 μm filtration ratings, but not a 5 μm carbon block filter. These results demonstrate that live, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae emerge from drowned snails and slugs, survive for extended periods of time in water, and may be able to enter a catchment user's household water supply. This study illustrates the need to better investigate and understand the potential role of contaminated water as a transmission route for neuroangiostrongyliasis.
</source>

text:
In this study, we explored the shifts in body composition, adipokines, and inflammatory markers following initial antiretroviral therapy (ART) with either a nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (N(t)RTI)-sparing or containing regimen. Our data comes from the NEAT 001/ANRS 143 trial, which compared darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) plus raltegravir (RAL) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) in 805 HIV-infected adults new to ART. The main goal was to see how limb fat percentage changed by week 96, with other targets being how these changes tied to metabolic markers like IL-6, insulin, leptin, adiponectin, and FGF-23.

Out of 805 participants, 126 were included in this substudy. Over 96 weeks, the rate of BMI change differed between groups, with a 1.5% per 48-week period increase for RAL versus TDF/FTC (p = 0.015). Changes in limb fat mass, trunk fat mass, total body fat, and total lean mass were 2.5% (p = 0.38), 7.3% (p = 0.021), 4.9% (p = 0.061), and 1.3% (p = 0.12), respectively. At the start, insulin and leptin levels were linked to limb and trunk fat mass. After adjustments, a 10% faster increase in leptin from baseline to week 48 was tied to a quicker increase in limb fat (0.5% per 48 weeks, p<0.001), total body fat mass (0.6% per 48 weeks, p<0.001), and trunk fat mass (0.3% per 48 weeks, p = 0.0026).

After 96 weeks, the N(t)RTI-sparing regimen of DRV/r + RAL led to a greater percentage increase in body composition variables, with significant changes in trunk fat mass and BMI.

 Farmer Boy is based on the childhood of husband, Almanzo Wilder, who grew up in the 1860s near the town of Malone in upstate New York. The book covers one year in Almanzo's life, beginning just before his ninth birthday, and describes in detail the endless chores involved in running the Wilder family farm. Young as he is, Almanzo rises before 5 a.m. every day to milk several cows and feed stock. In the growing season, he plants and tends crops; in winter, he hauls logs, helps fill the ice house, trains a team of young oxen, and sometimes—when his father can spare him—goes to school. The novel includes stories of Almanzo's brother Royal and his sisters Eliza Jane and Alice. While Laura Ingalls grows up in a little house on the western prairie, Almanzo Wilder is living on a big farm in New York State, where he and his brother and sisters work at their chores from dawn to dinner most days-no matter what the weather. There is still time for fun, though, especially with the horses, which Almanzo loves more than anything.
</source>

text:
Dairine, Nita's younger sister, stumbles upon Nita's copy of the Wizard's Manual and decides to take the Wizard's Oath herself. She's given her own Wizard's Manual in the form of a computer, which she affectionately nicknames "Spot." Using her newfound powers, Dairine jets off to Mars, then to the Crossings, where she's ambushed by agents of the Lone Power. Fleeing through a worldgate with the help of a mysterious man she meets in a bar, she ends up on a massive planet made entirely of silicon.

Meanwhile, Nita and Kit realize Dairine's gone missing and rush to her aid. Dairine wakes up a colossal computer embedded in the planet and starts designing and naming 'mobiles' as the planet begins creating quicklife (computer-based) creatures. She names them after everything from computer programs to Star Wars characters. When the Lone Power possesses one of these mobiles and attacks Dairine, Nita and Kit arrive just in time to assist her. They're aided by Machu Picchu (or Peach, as she's known), a macaw who reveals herself as the One's Champion incarnate. With Peach's help, they defeat the Lone Power by halting the universe's expansion. The resulting explosion of light obliterates the Lone Power, who's then taken home by one of the Powers That Be. As he leaves, he instructs Kit and Nita to destroy the remaining shadows he's left behind.

The universe continues its expansion, and Nita, Kit, and Dairine return home. There, Dairine's computer surprises them all by sprouting legs and following her upstairs as Nita and Kit fill their parents in on everything that's happened.

text:
FIFA, the governing body of football, suspended El Salvador from competing in all international football matches. The suspension came after the Salvadorian government refused to recognize football officials appointed by FIFA. This refusal led FIFA to view the situation as political interference.

Last year, Rodrigo Calvo, the head of the Salvadorian Football Association (FESFUT), resigned. FIFA then stepped in and appointed a special commission to reform the association's finances. However, Salvadorian President Mauricio Funes refused to acknowledge this commission.

The suspension impacts next month's World Cup in South Africa. Although El Salvador's national team did not qualify for the tournament, three Salvadorian referees were selected to participate. If the suspension is not lifted by the tournament's start, these referees will be unable to take part.

A meeting of FIFA's executive commission is scheduled for June 8. If the Salvadorian government does not reverse its stance by then, the suspension will become permanent. Consequently, El Salvador will remain suspended for the entire year, until the FIFA congress reconvenes in June 2011.

text:
So, there's this guy, Richard Collier, a 36-year-old screenwriter who's got some seriously bad news - an inoperable brain tumor. After flipping a coin, he decides to spend his remaining days at the famous Hotel del Coronado. He starts writing a journal, pouring out his thoughts and experiences.

Richard becomes totally fascinated by an old photograph of a famous stage actress, Elise McKenna, who performed at the hotel back in the 1890s. He digs up info about her life, learning that she never tied the knot, had this overprotective manager named William Fawcett Robinson, and had a brief fling with some mysterious guy during her stay in 1896.

The more Richard uncovers, the more he's convinced it's his destiny to time travel and become that mysterious man. After some research, he figures out a way to mentally transport himself back in time. It's a struggle, but he finally succeeds. At first, he's super disoriented and worried about snapping back to the present, but those feelings fade.

When he finally meets Elise, he's not sure what to say, but she surprises him by asking, "Is it you?" Turns out, two psychics told her she'd meet a mysterious man right then and there. Richard keeps his future origins a secret and starts a relationship with her, all while trying to adapt to the time's conventions. His daily headaches vanish, and he thinks his future memories might disappear too.

But Robinson, thinking Richard's after Elise's money, hires two guys to abduct Richard and leave him in a shed while Elise catches a train. Richard escapes and makes it back to the hotel, where he finds Elise never left. They share a passionate night together. In the middle of the night, Richard bumps into Robinson, and after a quick struggle, he runs back to the room. He pulls out a coin, realizing too late it's from the 1970s. The sight of it sends him back to the present.

At the end, we find out Richard passed away soon after. A doctor says the time-travel stuff was just Richard's mind playing tricks, a dying man's fantasy. But Richard's brother, who published the journal, isn't so sure.

On the first day of voting in Iraq's elections, two suicide bombers targeted polling stations in Baghdad, resulting in at least 14 deaths. These attacks took place during early voting, which allows certain groups like government employees, the sick, and prisoners to cast their ballots before the main elections on Sunday. The two incidents occurred approximately an hour apart in separate districts of Baghdad. According to official reports, at least 14 people lost their lives in these attacks, excluding the 31 killed in previous day's violence. However, unofficial accounts from the scene suggested that the actual death toll might be higher. Officials attributed these attacks to insurgents aiming to disrupt the elections, viewed as a crucial step in Iraq's efforts to achieve unity.

In anticipation of the elections and in response to insurgent threats, the Iraqi government had implemented significant security measures. This included detailed planning and collaboration with American military forces. Nevertheless, a senior government official acknowledged the ongoing risk of violence, stating that the possibility of further attacks remains until a stable government is established.

Washington Governor Christine Gregoire hasn't been messing around. She's gone and declared a state of emergency due to the crazy storms that've been rolling through. The National Guard's even been called in to help get supplies to folks who need them.

Now, if you're thinking about the bright lights of Seattle, they're mostly back to normal. But out in the rural areas and smaller communities, it's been a different story. Puget Sound Energy's got about 200,000 customers still without power out of the 700,000 who lost it. Seattle City Light's doing a bit better, with only 18,000 folks in the dark by Monday morning. That's down from a whopping 175,000, so things are looking up.

But it's not all good news. Sadly, there've been more casualties. Four more deaths have been reported, bringing the total to eight. A guy in Gig Harbor was walking his dog when he got zapped by a downed power line. In Spanaway, another man died when a candle started a house fire. And in Burien, a family of five lost one of their own due to carbon monoxide from an indoor generator. Even up in Canada, two folks in British Columbia passed away from the same thing. Hospitals are still seeing cases of CO poisoning, like a family in Shoreline who used an indoor grill. It seems people are putting noisy generators inside because of noise concerns from neighbors.

The Red Cross has been setting up shelters in King and other affected counties for those who've been left without power or food. Hotels are packed, with folks seeking warmth and a place to stay. Restaurants are seeing a lot of business too, as people look for a hot meal. And with all this, tons of food's probably gone bad due to the prolonged outage.

People without power are sticking with friends or family who've got it, or heading out of the area altogether. But traveling's been rough, with roadway lighting and services down. Most major roads that were closed during the storm are back open though. The 520 Floating Bridge has some minor damage, but it's still standing. Amtrak's Cascades service is back up and running, and Sea-Tac Airport's operating again, though with fewer flights after a power outage messed with their radar on Friday.

A state of emergency was declared Sunday for the U.S. state of Washington by governor Christine Gregoire, as additional reports of storm-related casualties surfaced. The state National Guard has been deployed to aid in distributing supplies.

Thousands were still without power in the coastal and Puget Sound regions, though most urban areas were back with power as late as Sunday afternoon, and outages were mostly contained to rural and unincorporated areas. Puget Sound Energy reported that roughly 500,000 energy customers out of the 700,000 who lost power were back in service by Sunday evening. Seattle City Light, the city's independent municipal utility, reported only 18,000 customers still without power as of Monday morning, down from a peak of 175,000.

Four additional deaths related to the post-storm power outage had been reported as of Monday, bringing the total number of casualties to eight. A man in Gig Harbor was electrocuted by a downed power line while walking his dog. Another man in Spanaway died when an unattended candle caused a house fire.

On Monday, four new carbon-monoxide deaths were reported in a family of five in Burien due to an indoor generator. In Canada, which had some damage from the week's storms, two southern British Columbia carbon monoxide deaths were also reported. Despite continued warnings, hospitals are still seeing cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, including a family in w:Shoreline, Washington which was taken to the hospital after they reported symptoms due to their indoor grill. Neighbors of the Burien family suggested that noise concerns are leading people to place noisy generators indoors.

The Red Cross set up shelters throughout King and other affected counties for those without power or food. Hotels reported no vacancies as whole families took shelter in powered hotels, especially in Seattle. Restaurants also reported brisk business as people sought out a hot cooked meal. Tons of perishable food were expected to have become unsafe after the prolonged outage disabled refrigerators and freezers both in homes and stores.

Many of those without power visited nearby friends and family living where power had been continued or restored, while others traveled out of the area to places that had not been affected. The widespread outage made long-distance traveling treacherous on some major routes, with roadway lighting, cellular towers, and services disabled by the outage.

Most major roadways which were closed during the storm were reopened on Friday. The 520 Floating Bridge over Lake Washington, a major conduit to the technology-rich Eastside, sustained minor damage. Amtrak, which had halted its Cascades service, resumed Saturday evening. Sea-Tac Airport resumed operations with a reduced flight load, after a transient power outage on Friday disabled the airport radar and caused all planes to be grounded until it was repaired.
</source>

text:
African populations exhibit a high degree of genetic diversity. This diversity may stem from natural selection pressures. Numerous studies have linked various genetic diversities to differences in susceptibility to infectious diseases, such as malaria. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the impact of genetic diversity when interpreting clinical trial results in malaria-endemic regions.

This study aimed to assess genetic polymorphism related to erythrocyte traits across different populations in malaria-endemic areas of Mali. Cross-sectional surveys were conducted among various ethnic groups residing in these areas. After obtaining informed consent, six milliliters of whole blood were collected from each participant in EDTA vials.

Phenotyping was performed for the ABO, Rh, Kell, MNSs, Kidd, and Duffy blood group systems using gel filtration techniques. A total of 231 subjects from six villages were included. The most frequent blood group phenotypes were O (40.7%) and A (31.2%), with corresponding allele frequencies of 0.65 and 0.21, respectively.

In the Rh system, the most common haplotypes were R0 (0.55), r (0.20), and R1 (0.13). Seven percent of participants were Duffy positive, and 4% exhibited Glycophorin B deficiency (S-s-). All participants tested negative for Kell.

The ABO and Rh systems demonstrated polymorphism among these Malian ethnic groups. These findings should be considered when evaluating susceptibility to malaria in clinical trials and when managing blood transfusion risks associated with malaria-induced anemia in children.

text:
The US government has arrested individuals alleged to be part of a Russian spy ring operating for several years. These agents, living under civilian identities, face charges of acting as unlawful agents for Russia, with a maximum sentence of five years. Additionally, nine suspects are charged with money laundering, which carries a penalty of up to twenty years in prison.

The FBI claims the suspects were trained by Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service to gather information on US military policies, particularly those related to nuclear weapons. They also targeted intelligence about leadership at the CIA and the White House.

To achieve their objectives, the suspects lived as American citizens under false names, with some posing as married couples. Notably, they established connections with influential US citizens, including a nuclear weapons scientist and a New York financier linked to US government officials.

Communication with Russian authorities allegedly employed various methods. These included unique wireless internet connections, internet pictures containing hidden messages, and traditional techniques like burying messages or exchanging bags between agents.

Names in quotes are cover names, while unquoted names are the alleged agents' real identities. Couples are listed together, and those living alone are separate. Arrests occurred at their respective locations.

The book was a source of the testimonies of Jewish children who were evacuated from the Soviet Union to Palestine. Grynberg arranged the “collection of interviews” to serve as a reminder about the Holocaust experience. The Polish children’s experiences during World War II also provided a recollection of their lives before the war. text:
Ecuador secured a 2-0 victory over Poland in their second Group A match at the soccer World Cup, thanks to a robust defensive effort and two well-executed goals. The match took place at the Veltins-Arena stadium in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, where thousands of Polish fans witnessed their team's struggles to mount effective attacks.

The first half began cautiously, with neither team able to create a scoring opportunity in the opening 20 minutes. Ecuador broke the deadlock when Carlos Tenario capitalized on a throw-in from the right, heading the ball past Polish goalkeeper Artur Boruc into the far corner of the net. Ecuador's captain and defender Ivan Hurtado, who was later substituted due to injury in the 67th minute, played a crucial role in this defensive effort.

In the second half, Poland dominated possession as Ecuador focused on preserving their lead and launching counterattacks. However, Poland's struggles continued as they frequently misplaced passes and lost possession in the final third of the pitch. Ecuador doubled their lead ten minutes from time when Polish defenders mishandled the ball, leading to a two-on-one situation that Ecuador capitalized on, with Boruc unable to prevent the goal.

Poland's manager, Pawel Janas, saw his team's offensive efforts finally gain traction in the last five minutes, with shots hitting both the crossbar and the post of Ecuador's goalkeeper Christian Mora's goal. The strong defensive performance by Ecuador, particularly from Giovanny Espinoza and Ivan Hurtado, was instrumental in their victory. Ecuador will hope that Hurtado recovers in time for their next match against Costa Rica, while Poland faces a tough challenge against Germany, who won their opening World Cup game on Friday.

text:
This study aimed to evaluate the survival rates of Polish women diagnosed with cervical cancer (CC) and their adherence to treatment recommendations. Given that Polish medical societies' guidelines for CC management align with both European Society of Gynaecological Oncology (ESGO) and international standards, and considering that Poland's CC mortality rate is 70% higher than the EU average, we hypothesized discrepancies in treatment implementation.

We conducted a retrospective multicenter analysis of medical records from 1247 CC patients who completed at least two years of follow-up. Our findings revealed that, for FIGO IB to IVA CC patients, where concurrent radiotherapy and chemotherapy is the standard treatment in enhanced- and maximum-resource settings, the percentage of women receiving chemotherapy in Poland was lower than in countries with higher total survival rates.

However, for FIGO IA to IIA patients, treatment methods adhered to American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) guidelines, reflective of high-standard care countries. The observed inconsistencies in chemotherapy application, coupled with flaws in the cervical cancer screening program, may contribute to the poorer survival rates among Polish women with CC. This study highlights the need for further investigation into the factors influencing treatment adherence and patient outcomes in Poland.

text:
This mixed-methods review aims to explore how women's experiences of traveling for abortion have been studied, with a particular focus on travel distance, costs, delays, and other barriers to accessing services. Given the increasing restrictions on abortion providers and the subsequent rise in travel requirements for these services worldwide, this systematic examination of the literature is both timely and necessary.

Our search spanned several databases, including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Popline, and Google Scholar, initially in July 2016 and again in March 2017. We focused on original research that detailed women's experiences traveling for abortion. Two reviewers independently screened articles, extracted data, and determined final inclusion for analysis. The quality of the studies was assessed using CASP, STROBE, and MMAT checklists.

We found 59 relevant publications, comprising 46 quantitative studies, 12 qualitative studies, and 1 mixed-methods study. Most of these were published in the last five years and primarily relied on data from the US, with travel often being a secondary outcome of interest. Quantitative studies typically measured travel as the road or straight-line distance to an abortion provider. Some also considered the burdens of travel, such as financial costs, childcare needs, and the risk of unwanted disclosure of abortion status.

Qualitative studies delved into regional disparities in access to abortion care, the impact of travel on the choice of abortion method, and the reasons women travel. While the studies were generally of high quality, many lacked details on participant recruitment or consideration of potential biases.

To facilitate comparisons across studies, we recommend standardized measurements of travel, including associated burdens and more detailed considerations of travel costs. Further research is needed to accurately capture the various dimensions of the burden of travel for abortion services on women's lives.

To systematically review the literature on women’s experiences traveling for abortion and assess how this concept has been explored and operationalized, with a focus on travel distance, cost, delays, and other barriers to receiving services.

Increasing limitations on abortion providers and access to care have increased the necessity of travel for abortion services around the world. No systematic examination of women’s experiences traveling for abortion has been conducted; this mixed-methods review provides a summary of the qualitative and quantitative literature on this topic.

A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Popline, and Google Scholar in July 2016 and updated in March 2017 (PROSPERO registration # CRD42016046007). We included original research studies that described women’s experiences traveling for abortion. Two reviewers independently performed article screening, data extraction and determination of final inclusion for analysis. Critical appraisal was conducted using CASP, STROBE, and MMAT checklists.

Most studies were published in the last five years, relied on data from the US, and discussed travel as a secondary outcome of interest. In quantitative studies, travel was primarily conceptualized and measured as road or straight-line distance to abortion provider, though some studies also incorporated measures of burdens related to travel, such as financial cost, childcare needs, and unwanted disclosure of their abortion status to others. Qualitative studies explored regional disparities in access to abortion care, with a focus on the burdens related to travel, the impact of travel on abortion method choice, and women’s reasons for travel. Studies generally were of high quality, though many studies lacked information on participant recruitment or consideration of potential biases.

Standardized measurements of travel, including burdens associated with travel and more nuanced considerations of travel costs, should be implemented in order to facilitate comparison across studies. More research is needed to explore and accurately capture different dimensions of the burden of travel for abortion services on women’s lives.

text: The parasitic infection neuroangiostrongyliasis, attributed to the nematode Angiostrongylus cantonensis, has been documented in Hawaiʻi since the mid-20th century. Recent observations indicate a rise in cases, notably in East Hawaiʻi Island, coinciding with the establishment of the invasive semi-slug Parmarion martensi. In regions lacking conventional water infrastructure, households rely on rainwater catchment systems for domestic water, which currently evade federal, state, or county regulation. Despite known risks of waterborne contamination by gastropods and subsequent infection, this transmission pathway remains unaddressed by regulatory authorities. This research investigates four key aspects: (1) the emergence of viable, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae from submerged, non-indigenous, detrimental gastropods; (2) the distribution of larvae in undisturbed water columns; (3) the lifespan of free-living larvae in water; and (4) the efficacy of rainwater catchment filters in impeding infective-stage larvae. Larvae were expelled from both minced and whole gastropods submerged in either municipal water or rainwater, with approximately 94% of larvae detected at the water column's base 72–96 hours post-submersion. Infective-stage larvae maintained activity for 21 days in municipal water. Histological analysis of P. martensi revealed nematode larvae in close proximity to the gastropod's body wall, supporting the potential for larval discharge via slime. Gastropod tissue squashes proved effective as a rapid screening method. Neuroangiostrongyliasis, caused by Angiostrongylus cantonensis, has been reported in Hawaiʻi since the 1950's. An increase in cases is being reported primarily from East Hawaiʻi Island, correlated with the introduction of the semi-slug Parmarion martensi. Households in areas lacking infrastructure for water must use rainwater catchment as their primary domestic water supply, for which there is no federal, state, or county regulation. Despite evidence that slugs and snails can contaminate water and cause infection, regulatory bodies have not addressed this potential transmission route. This study evaluates: 1) the emergence of live, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae from drowned, non-native, pestiforous gastropods; 2) larvae location in an undisturbed water column; 3) longevity of free-living larvae in water; and 4) effectiveness of rainwater catchment filters in blocking infective-stage larvae. Infective-stage larvae were active for 21 days in municipal water. Histological sectioning of P. martensi showed proximity of nematode larvae to the body wall of the gastropod, consistent with the potential for shedding of larvae in slime. Gastropod tissue squashes showed effectivity as a quick screening method. Live, infective-stage larvae were able to traverse rainwater catchment polypropylene sediment filters of 20 μm, 10 μm, 5 μm, and 1 μm filtration ratings, but not a 5 μm carbon block filter. These results demonstrate that live, infective-stage A. cantonensis larvae emerge from drowned snails and slugs, survive for extended periods of time in water, and may be able to enter a catchment user's household water supply. This study illustrates the need to better investigate and understand the potential role of contaminated water as a transmission route for neuroangiostrongyliasis.

text:
Buster Casey, born in the quiet town of Middleton, was no ordinary kid. He had an incredible sense of smell and taste, way more powerful than anyone else's. He earned the nickname "Rant" after a childhood prank involving animal organs that made a whole bunch of people sick. As they were vomiting, they made a sound that sounded like "rant," and that's how he got his nickname.

As a kid, Rant stumbled upon a massive fortune that completely changed his small town's economy. But that wasn't weird enough—he became obsessed with getting bitten by rabid animals and venomous snakes and spiders. After his first black widow bite, he discovered something unexpected: the toxin gave him an erection. He used this to skip school, even threatening his way to an early diploma and a big fat check to leave town.

When Rant hit the city, things took a dystopian turn. The city was split into Daytimers and Nighttimers, with the Nighttimers living under oppressive curfews. Rant became a Nighttimer and got swept up in "Party Crashing," a dangerous game of demolition derby played on city streets at night. The goal? Crash into other players' cars that had specific "flags," like a Christmas tree or "Just Married" written on the windshield.

He met Echo Lawrence, a fellow crasher and the love of his life. But Rant also sparked a nationwide rabies epidemic that spiraled out of control, leading to zombie-like outbreaks where the infected were shot on sight. Eventually, Rant died during a Party Crashing event, broadcast live on national TV and radio. But here's the weird part—when they opened his car, his body was gone.

After his "death," people speculated about what happened. Some thought that crashing a car in a certain state of mind could take you out of time, letting you kill your ancestors and become immortal. Others believed you could use incest to become something more than human—something they suspected happened to Green Taylor Simms, another Party Crasher with shady ties to Rant.

After he stops taking medication prescribed by his psychiatrist, his depression builds up until, unable to fend off his suicidal ideation, he calls 1-800-SUICIDE and is admitted to a nearby psychiatric hospital. He meets many other patients, some friendly, others reclusive or delusional, and is supported and encouraged by his family and school principal once they learn of his hospitalization. Craig meets Noelle, a female patient who coped with a history of sexual abuse by cutting her face with scissors. In isolation from the outside world, and with help from Noelle, Craig confronts the sources of his anxiety and regains his health. During his recovery, Craig experiments with art, specifically stylized maps, and discovers he has a great deal of natural talent and ability. Once Craig has recovered, his counselor suggests he transfer to an art school, a thought that excites Craig. At the end of the novel, having undergone a mental "shift", he returns home. He narrates that his brain now tells him that he wants to "live", and he says he now wants to "do". He then begins to list the things he wants to do, such as eat, sleep, run, walk, kiss, and read, among others.

text: A secret summit of superpowers is to be held in Baghdad, but it is no longer secret, and a shadowy fascist group is plotting to sabotage the event. Things get complicated when enthusiastic young tourist Victoria Jones discovers a dying secret British agent Henry "Fakir" Carmichael in her hotel room, his last words - "Lucifer...Basrah...Lefarge" - propel her into investigation. "Lucifer" refers to the mastermind, Victoria's false lover Edward, who is behind the plot. "Basrah" refers to the city where certain documents were handed to certain people. "Lefarge" turns out to actually be "Defarge" and is a reference to a Charles Dickens character; it is a clue to where the aforementioned documents can be found. An interesting comparison can be made between the romance themes of this novel and The Man in the Brown Suit, which is also primarily an adventure novel, rather than a straight whodunnit. In that book, the exciting, mysterious young man that falls into the heroine's room ends up as the romantic hero. In Baghdad, an exciting, mysterious young man also falls into the heroine's room, but he is disposed of, as is the other exciting, mysterious young man that the heroine has followed to Baghdad. A more conventional and staid archaeologist ends up as the romantic hero; Christie herself was married to archaeologist Max Mallowan by this date.

text: Dirk and Martha Lawrence are apparently not the happiest couple in New York, despite her millions of dollars and his fairly successful mystery-writing career. Martha asks for a secretive meeting to get Ellery Queen's advice because Dirk's violent jealousy is causing problems in her life—but Dirk shows up suspecting the worst and punches Ellery into unconsciousness. Dirk apologizes the next day, telling the story of how his father had killed his mother's lover, thereby causing his over-reaction. Ellery's secretary and inamorata Nikki Porter urges him to stay involved in the situation and Nikki moves in with the Lawrences to keep an eye on things (and act as Dirk's secretary on a stalled book). Nikki soon reports that Martha actually is having a series of clandestine meetings with romantic actor Van Harrison. The meetings are arranged with innocuous envelopes that look like advertising, but with Martha's name and address written in scarlet typewriter ink. Also, the envelopes contain only a day, time and a sequential letter of the alphabet—a code that is soon linked to a New York Guidebook. By the time the meetings have progressed from "A" through to "W", Dirk has found out about the affair and followed Martha to Van's home in the suburb of Darien. He breaks in, confronts the pair and shoots them both, seriously wounding Martha, who nearly dies. Van Harrison has just enough time before he dies to leave a dying clue—using his own blood, he writes an "X", then a "Y" on the wall, and dies. Ellery must consider the significance of this dying message and finally solves it, just as Dirk's murder trial is about to conclude. After Ellery gets a private conversation with the judge, a criminal then receives justice.

text:
To evaluate the long-term cumulative probability of intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation with the intravitreal dexamethasone implant (IDI) when used to treat different indications: diabetic macular edema, uveitis, retinal vein occlusion.

705 IDI injections (429 eyes) were assessed and Kaplan-Meier graphs were generated to assess: the probability of different levels of IOP elevation (IOP≥21, ≥25 or ≥35 mmHg), IOP change ≥10 mmHg, initiation of IOP-lowering treatment, glaucoma surgery, IOP change with repeat injections and IOP elevation in eyes with glaucoma and ocular hypertension (OHT).

The cumulative probability of IOP ≥21, ≥25 and ≥35 mmHg was 50%-60%, 25%-30% and 6%-7% at 12–24 months, respectively. The probability of initiating IOP-lowering medication was 31%-54% at 12–24 months. Glaucoma and OHT eyes had a higher probability of mild IOP elevation (≥21 mmHg, 65.1%, 75% and 57.8%, p = 0.01), yet a similar moderate (≥25 mmHg, 22.3%, 28% and 30.2%, p = 0.91) and severe elevation of IOP (≥35 mmHg, 3.7%, 7.1% and 4%, p = 0.71) as normal eyes. Glaucoma surgery was required in only 0.9% cases (4/429). At baseline, 8.8% of the treated eyes had glaucoma, 6.7% OHT and 16.9% were already on IOP-lowering medication.

In the long-term (24 months), IOP elevation is common, generally mild (30% IOP, ≥25 mmHg) and well-tolerated, resolving with topical treatment (54%) and rarely requiring surgery (0.9%).

text: Spasticity is an important barrier that can hinder the restoration of function in stroke patients. Although several studies have attempted to elucidate the relationship between brain lesions and spasticity, the effects of specific brain lesions on the development of spasticity remain unclear. Thus, the present study investigated the effects of stroke lesions on spasticity in stroke patients. The present retrospective longitudinal observational study assessed 45 stroke patients using the modified Ashworth Scale to measure muscle spasticity. Each patient was assessed four times: initially (within 2 weeks of stroke) and at 1, 3, and 6 months after the onset of stroke. Brain lesions were analyzed using voxel-based lesion symptom mapping (VLSM) with magnetic resonance imaging images. Spasticity developed to a certain degree within 3 months in most stroke patients with spasticity. The VLSM method with non-parametric mapping revealed that lesions in the superior corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, posterior corona radiata, thalamus, putamen, premotor cortex, and insula were associated with the development of upper-limb spasticity. Additionally, lesions of the superior corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, posterior corona radiata, thalamus, putamen, and external capsule were associated with the development of lower-limb spasticity. The present study identified several brain lesions that contributed to post-stroke spasticity. Specifically, the involvement of white matter tracts and the striatum influenced the development of spasticity in the upper and lower limbs of stroke patients. These results may be useful for planning rehabilitation strategies and for understanding the pathophysiology of spasticity in stroke patients.

text: A new dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) method is introduced for simultaneous system identification and denoising in conjunction with the adoption of an extended Kalman filter algorithm. The present paper explains the extended-Kalman-filter-based DMD (EKFDMD) algorithm which is an online algorithm for dataset for a small number of degree of freedom (DoF). It also illustrates that EKFDMD requires significant numerical resources for many-degree-of-freedom (many-DoF) problems and that the combination with truncated proper orthogonal decomposition (trPOD) helps us to apply the EKFDMD algorithm to many-DoF problems, though it prevents the algorithm from being fully online. The numerical experiments of a noisy dataset with a small number of DoFs illustrate that EKFDMD can estimate eigenvalues better than or as well as the existing algorithms, whereas EKFDMD can also denoise the original dataset online. In particular, EKFDMD performs better than existing algorithms for the case in which system noise is present. The EKFDMD with trPOD, which unfortunately is not fully online, can be successfully applied to many-DoF problems, including a fluid-problem example, and the results reveal the superior performance of system identification and denoising.

text: Ocean warming has facilitated the range expansion of commercially important sea urchin species to higher latitudes. Heliocidaris crassispina was recorded to extend northward to Toga Bay along the Oga Peninsula, Japan following an increase in seawater temperatures, and replacement of local sea urchin species Mesocentrotus nudus. In order to identify evidence of adaptation occurring in response to a range extension of H. crassispina to the newly extended environments, we randomly collected 106 H. crassispina in August 2014 in Toga Bay, determined the growth and age composition and examined gonad traits (size, color and development). To confirm the gonad development, 30 H. crassispina with > 30 mm diameter were collected in July, August and September 2017. We found slower growth in the extended range than the central range. More delayed gonad development of males than those of females and a large variety of developmental stages in the acini of testis indicated that the spawning of both sexes of the sea urchins were asynchronous. In terms of gonad color, L* (lightness) values increased with increasing GI, while b* (yellowness) values decreased with increasing age. The population consisted of seven year-classes from 2006 to 2012, suggesting persistent juvenile recruitment. Long-term water temperature data indicated that the range extension of H. crassispina was due to ocean warming, in particular during the summer spawning season.

text:
HIV-infected adults receiving anti-retroviral therapy have a high prevalence of food insecurity in both high- and low-income settings., Women bear an inequitable burden of food insecurity due to lack of control over resources and over household food allocation decision-making. The few studies conducted on the association between food insecurity and gender among HIV-infected adults have inconclusive findings. Therefore, the objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled effect of gender on food insecurity among HIV-infected adults receiving antiretroviral therapy.

We conducted an electronic, web-based search using PubMed, CINAHL, PopLine, MedNar, Embase, Cochrane library, the JBI Library, the Web of Science and Google Scholar. We included studies which reported the association between food insecurity and gender among HIV-infected adults receiving antiretroviral therapy whose age was greater than 18 years. The analysis was conducted using STATA 14 software. A random effects model was used to estimate the pooled effect a 95% confidence interval(CI). Forest plots were used to visualize the presence of heterogeneity. Funnel plots and Egger’s and Begg’s tests were used to check for publication bias.

A total of 776 studies were identified of which seventeen studies were included in the meta-analysis, with a total of 5827 HIV infected adults receiving antiretroviral therapy. We found that the gender of HIV-infected adults receiving anti-retroviral therapy had statistically significant effects on food insecurity. The pooled odds of developing food insecurity among female HIV infected adults receiving anti-retroviral therapy was 53% higher than male HIV infected adults (OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.29, 1.83). Our analysis indicate the findings of studies conducted in the high-income countries showed weakest associations between gender and food insecurity than those conducted in low- and middle-income countries.

Our systematic review and meta-analysis showed statistically significant effect of gender on food insecurity among HIV-infected adults receiving anti-retroviral therapy in which odds of food insecurity was higher among female HIV infected adults compared to male HIV-infected adults. These findings suggest that the need to include within food and nutrition interventions for HIV-infected adults receiving antiretroviral treatment, culture- and context-specific gender-based policies to address the sex/gender related vulnerability to food insecurity.

text:
The failure rate of epidural anesthesia using the loss of resistance technique is 13–23%.

To investigate the efficacy of epidural electric stimulation-guided epidural analgesia in vaginal delivery.

An open label randomized prospective study.

Laboring women were randomized to two groups: epidural catheter insertion using only a loss of resistance technique or a loss of resistance technique with confirmation by electric stimulation. Catheters in both groups were initially tested with 3 ml of 1% lidocaine and those with any evidence of motor blockade were considered intrathecal. Sensory blockade and an 11 point numerical rating score for pain were assessed 30 minutes after administration of an epidural bolus of 10 ml of 0.22% ropivacaine with fentanyl. Successful epidural analgesia was defined as a decrease of 2 or more in the pain score and a bilateral L1-T10 sensory blockade.

Thirty-one patients were randomized to each group. The first 20 patients in each group were enrolled in a pilot study and were also included in the final analysis. One patient in the electric stimulation group was excluded owing to dural puncture by the Tuohy needle. One patient in each group demonstrated motor blockade after test dose and were considered failures. The number (% (95% confidence interval)) of successful cases were 29 out of 30 (97% (85, 100%)) in the electric stimulation group and 24 out of 31 (77% (61, 89%)) in the loss of resistance group (P = 0.053). However, analysis of only patients with absence of motor blockade revealed that 29 out of 29 (100% (92, 100%)) patients in the electric stimulation group and 24 of 29 (80% (63, 91%)) patients in the loss of resistance group had adequate analgesia (P = 0.024).

Although limited by lack of blinding, small study size and inclusion of pilot study data, this study suggests epidural electric stimulation improves the success rate of subsequent labor analgesia.

text: We characterized 419 Mycoplasma pneumoniae isolates collected between 2011 and 2017 in Osaka prefecture of Japan. This analysis revealed high prevalence of macrolide-resistant M. pneumoniae (MRMP) in Osaka during 2011 and 2014 with annual detection rates of MRMP strains between 71.4% and 81.8%. However, in 2015 and after, the detection rate of MRMP decreased significantly and did not exceed 50%. Genotyping of the p1 gene of these isolates showed that most of MRMP strains harbored type 1 p1 gene. In contrast, strains expressing p1 gene type 2 or its variant were largely macrolide-susceptible M. pneumoniae (MSMP) strains. There was a strong correlation between p1 gene genotype and the presence of mutations conferring macrolide resistance in M. pneumoniae isolated in Osaka. These results indicate that lower incidence of MRMP strains in Osaka from 2015 was associated with the relative increase of p1 gene type 2 lineage strains. During these experiments, we also isolated three M. pneumoniae strains that showed irregular typing pattern in the polymerase chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) analysis of the p1 gene. Two of these strains harbored new variants of type 2 p1 gene and were designated as type 2f and 2g. The remaining strain with an irregular typing pattern had a large deletion in the p1 operon.
