text:
Each year, the Edinburgh Festival Fringe commences with its signature Cavalcade, a vibrant procession led by over 3,000 participants. Recent data estimate that roughly 160,000 individuals tune in to witness this spectacle. Festival director Gudgin advised viewers to approach the sprawling program with discernment, noting that it would take just under five and a half years, eleven months, and sixteen days of non-stop attendance to see every single show in sequence. The festivities are set to conclude on August 28th this year.

Economic impact studies conducted by Edinburgh City Council estimate that the Fringe contributes over £75 million to the local economy annually. This economic benefit is supported by a wide array of jobs ranging from rickshaw drivers and show announcers to crowds control personnel distributing flyers and collecting discarded materials from the streets. The festival's venues, including the Assembly venue on George Street and the 800-seat Assembly Hall on the Royal Mile, reported selling 97,000 tickets by the last Friday prior to the festival's close—a figure that surpasses the attendance records set in 1999.

Among the many performances, international and cross-cultural comedy and drama take center stage. Notable acts include Danish-Egyptian comedian Omar Marzouk, who addresses sensitive topics such as the controversy surrounding depictions of the Prophet Mohammed. At the same time, religious programming continues to be a significant presence, with events like Bible Babel Live! offering the complete text of the Bible in English, Greek, and Chinese over a 10-day, 80-hour marathon.

The religious component is underscored by the concurrent Festival of Spirituality and Peace, reflecting a noticeable surge in public interest in faith and spirituality. This trend is further influenced by legislative changes in the UK, notably the Racial and Religious Hatred Act, which aims to ensure equal legal protection for all faiths. Some comedians, including Rowan Atkinson, have expressed concern that such legislation could restrict the freedom of satire and comedic critique.

The arts scene also features provocative works. For example, Abie Philbin Bowman’s one-man show “Jesus: The Guantanamo Years” portrays Jesus as a bearded Middle Eastern man arrested by U.S. officials and held at Guantanamo, exploring themes of religious martyrdom. Other productions include “The Black Jew Dialogues,” “According to Jesus,” and “Situation Comedy,” a daring Israeli play addressing the complex realities of suicide bombings inspired by real events. Surrealist theater such as “Breasts and Burgers,” adapted from Guillaume Apollinaris’s 20th-century work, features the American flag literally torn aspart each night, drawing debate over its potential impact on American communities, particularly in the U.S. consulate’s view.

Logistical challenges have arisen as well. Actor Mel Smith, portraying Winston Churchill in “Allegiance,” had to abstain from smoking his signature cigar in Scotland’s smoke-free public spaces, as officials were prepared to close the Assembly Rooms if he violated the new regulations. These and other practical concerns have underscored the ongoing negotiation between artistic expression and public policy.

With a growing demand for cultural offerings and heightened awareness of social and legal issues, organizers are calling for increased funding from both public and private sectors to sustain and expand the festival’s reach and diversity in the coming years.

text: Despite advances in combating undernutrition, Africa remains at the forefront of global undernutrition rates, a situation further complicated by recurrent droughts and conflict. Mobile phones are increasingly being leveraged as a cost-effective platform for large-scale, rapid data collection across the continent, owing to the region’s rapid expansion in mobile subscriptions and ownership. To evaluate the feasibility and potential biases of using computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) via mobile phones to gather nutrition data, we conducted a one-week test-retest study involving 1,821 households in Kenya. We assessed Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women (MDD-W) and Minimum Acceptable Diet for Infants and Young Children (MAD) using both CATI and traditional face-to-face (F2F) survey methods. Our findings reveal that CATI was successfully completed for 75% (n = 1,366) of participants. While women’s reported MDD-W scores showed no significant difference between modalities, children’s scores indicated a notable increase in both dietary diversity (mean rise of 0.45 food groups; 95% CI 0.34–0.56) and meal frequency (mean increase of 0.75 meals per day; 95% CI 0.53–0.96) when assessed via CATI, translating to a 17% higher inferred prevalence of adequate diets among infants and young children. However, non-coverage bias due to participants without mobile access—primarily older and less asset-secured women—was modest (1–7%). Overall, utilizing mobile phones for nutrition data collection in African rural settings may yield estimates ranging from no change to as much as 25% higher than traditional in-person approaches.

text: To assess the long-term cumulative probability of intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation following intravitreal dexamethasone implant (IDI) use in patients with diabetic macular edema, uveitis, or retinal vein occlusion, a cohort of 429 eyes receiving 705 IDI injections was analyzed over 12–24 months. Kaplan-Meier curves evaluated the likelihood of IOP reaching ≥21 mmHg (50%–60%), ≥25 mmHg (25%–30%), or ≥35 mmHg (6%–7%) at 12–24 months. The probability of initiating IOP-lowering medication ranged from 31% to 54% during this period. Among eyes with pre-existing glaucoma or ocular hypertension (OHT), IOP elevation to ≥21 mmHg was more common (65.1%, 75%, and 57.8% for the three thresholds, p=0.01), though moderate (≥25 mmHg) and severe (≥35 mmHg) elevations were comparable across groups (p=0.91 and p=0.71, respectively). Only 0.9% (4 eyes) underwent glaucoma surgery over the study period. At baseline, 8.8% of eyes had glaucoma, 6.7% had OHT, and 16.9% were already on IOP-lowering medication. Overall, IOP elevation was common in the long term, typically mild (≈30% at ≥25 mmHg), often controlled with topical therapy (54% cases), and required surgery in less than 1% of eyes.

To evaluate the long-term cumulative probability of intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation with the intravitreal dexamethasone implant (IDI) when used to treat different indications: diabetic macular edema, uveitis, retinal vein occlusion.

705 IDI injections (429 eyes) were assessed and Kaplan-Meier graphs were generated to assess: the probability of different levels of IOP elevation (IOP≥21, ≥25 or ≥35 mmHg), IOP change ≥10 mmHg, initiation of IOP-lowering treatment, glaucoma surgery, IOP change with repeat injections and IOP elevation in eyes with glaucoma and ocular hypertension (OHT).

The cumulative probability of IOP ≥21, ≥25 and ≥35 mmHg was 50%-60%, 25%-30% and 6%-7% at 12–24 months, respectively. The probability of initiating IOP-lowering medication was 31%-54% at 12–24 months. Glaucoma and OHT eyes had a higher probability of mild IOP elevation (≥21 mmHg, 65.1%, 75% and 57.8%, p = 0.01), yet a similar moderate (≥25 mmHg, 22.3%, 28% and 30.2%, p = 0.91) and severe elevation of IOP (≥35 mmHg, 3.7%, 7.1% and 4%, p = 0.71) as normal eyes. Glaucoma surgery was required in only 0.9% cases (4/429). At baseline, 8.8% of the treated eyes had glaucoma, 6.7% OHT and 16.9% were already on IOP-lowering medication.

In the long-term (24 months), IOP elevation is common, generally mild (30% IOP, ≥25 mmHg) and well-tolerated, resolving with topical treatment (54%) and rarely requiring surgery (0.9%).
</source>

text: Increased ocean temperatures have enabled the northern extension of the range of Heliocidaris crassispina along the Oga Peninsula, Japan, replacing its local competitor, Mesocentrotus nudus. Analysis of 106 H. crassispina collected in Toga Bay in 2014 revealed slower growth rates in the newly expanded northern range compared to the central distribution. Gonad traits, including size, color (measured as lightness (L*) and yellowness (b*)), and developmental stage, were assessed. Male gonad development lagged behind that of females, and both sexes exhibited asynchronous spawning as indicated by variation in testicular acini maturity. The population comprised seven year-classes from 2006 to 2012, pointing to ongoing and sustained recruitment into the new habitat. Historical temperature records confirm that this northern shift primarily resulted from summer warming. Overall, these findings suggest that while H. crassispina has extended its range due to climate change, its northern populations display adaptive shifts in growth and reproduction, yet still maintain asynchronous breeding and slower growth compared to previous ranges.

<source>
Ocean warming has facilitated the range expansion of commercially important sea urchin species to higher latitudes. Heliocidaris crassispina was recorded to extend northward to Toga Bay along the Oga Peninsula, Japan following an increase in seawater temperatures, and replacement of local sea urchin species Mesocentrotus nudus. In order to identify evidence of adaptation occurring in response to a range extension of H. crassispina to the newly extended environments, we randomly collected 106 H. crassispina in August 2014 in Toga Bay, determined the growth and age composition and examined gonad traits (size, color and development). To confirm the gonad development, 30 H. crassispina with > 30 mm diameter were collected in July, August and September 2017. We found slower growth in the extended range than the central range. More delayed gonad development of males than those of females and a large variety of developmental stages in the acini of testis indicated that the spawning of both sexes of the sea urchins were asynchronous. In terms of gonad color, L* (lightness) values increased with increasing GI, while b* (yellowness) values decreased with increasing age. The population consisted of seven year-classes from 2006 to 2012, suggesting persistent juvenile recruitment. Long-term water temperature data indicated that the range extension of H. crassispina was due to ocean warming, in particular during the summer spawning season.
</source>

Craig is a fifteen-year-old high school student from an upper-middle-class family in Manhattan. He lives in a bustling city neighborhood and attends Executive Pre-Professional High School, where he has worked hard to get in. There, the pressure is intense—not only academically, but also because he secretly pines for Nia, Aaron’s girlfriend and someone he can’t have. These stresses, along with mounting expectations, soon take a serious toll on Craig’s mental health. He battles eating disorders, struggles with depression, uses marijuana to cope, has disrupted sleep, and is plagued by dark thoughts about ending his life. After his prescribed psychiatric medication wears off, his feelings grow unmanageable, leading him to contact the 1-800-SUICIDE crisis line and enter a nearby psychiatric hospital.

While in the hospital, Craig encounters a mix of fellow patients—some are welcoming, others withdrawn or even delusional. Through these encounters, he finds moments of connection and receives the support he desperately needs from his family and the school principal, who reach out when they hear about his situation. Among the patients is Noelle, who survived sexual abuse by harming herself with scissors. In the hospital’s quiet isolation, Craig, with Noelle’s help, begins to face his own anxiety head-on and slowly starts to recover.

During his healing process, Craig discovers a new outlet: creating stylized maps. This artistic expression uncovers a hidden talent within him. When his counselor suggests he consider transferring to an art school, Craig feels a renewed sense of possibility and purpose. By the novel’s end, after a mental shift—referred to as a “brain reset”—he has changed his mind. He no longer sees himself as trapped by his problems. Now, Craig’s thoughts are focused on what he wants to live for: the simple, vital things like eating, sleeping, running, walking, kissing, and reading. He looks to the future with hope and a sense of direction, ready to move forward.

A car bomb detonated early Monday morning near a military academy in Santona, northern Spain, resulting in the death of a soldier and injuries to several others. Authorities attribute the attack to the Basque separatist group ETA. This incident marks the third car bombing in 24 hours, all believed to have been orchestrated by ETA.

These incidents occur amid heightened tension in Basque politics. Recently, Spanish courts have banned two Basque nationalist political parties due to alleged links to ETA and have incarcerated 21 individuals associated with the group. The attacks underscore ongoing unrest and the continued risk posed by ETA.

text:
After his harrowing ordeal, Dannerman begins a slow but determined recovery, during which he uncovers more about the Horch and the enigmatic Beloved Leaders—and the other species caught up in the ongoing war. Driven by a sense of urgency, he scours the surroundings for useful information and advanced technology that could help him get back to Earth and deliver a warning to the human authorities. His main goal remains: to find a way home before the Beloved Leaders arrive in force.

When approached to aid in preparing one of the recently liberated prisoners for a dangerous infiltration mission among the Beloved Leaders, Dannerman sees his chance to escape. He outlines the plan to his hosts, the Horch, hoping to persuade them with cleverness rather than force. Despite their initial refusal, he manages to talk his way into proceeding, thanks in part to his quick wit and the situation’s tension.

Soon, Dannerman finds himself aboard a stealth submarine hidden beneath the ocean’s surface near Earth. There, he manages to reach out to human authorities. To his surprise, his government already knows about the Beloved Leaders and is actively on guard—but they apparently haven’t detected the submarines lurking beneath. This gives him a sliver of hope.

Soon after, Dannerman and his alien companions are questioned again by U.S. officials and UN representatives, but the tone is much more measured this time. Because he still carries a translation implant from the Beloved Leaders, Dannerman serves as the vital interpreter, bridging the language gap and the cultural divide. With his guidance and the assistance of Horch technology, the submarines carrying the Beloved Leaders are located and disabled before they can release their usual weapon of underwater methane—part of the invaders’ standard tactic when facing unyielding worlds.

Having survived these perilous events, the President of the United States decides to make the encounter public, ensuring the world is informed and ready to defend itself should the Beloved Leaders return. Dannerman’s story, and the knowledge he’s provided, could be humanity’s best chance at survival in the ongoing struggle.

text:
The European Commission could impose a penalty as high as 5 percent of Microsoft’s daily revenue—an amount equivalent to about $5 million per day—should the company fail to comply with its regulatory requirements. This potential fine stems from an investigation launched in 2003-2004 over Microsoft’s practice of pre-instolving Windows Media Player with Windows OS, a move the European Commission accused of unfairly undercutting competitors. The investigation had previously led to negotiations that broke down in March 2004, resulting in Microsoft’s record fine of €497 million (about $613 million) for violations of EU competition law.

After that fine, Microsoft was required to ship versions of Windows without the integrated Windows Media Player and to license many of its key protocols to software developers across the European Economic Area. However, the commission recently declined Microsoft’s proposal to license its workgroup server protocols on a per-server basis. The decision was influenced by criticism from the Free Software Foundation Europe, which argued that such a licensing model would hinder the development of free software, given that it is impossible to accurately estimate the number of free software users or servers in Europe. Microsoft, meanwhile, continues to search for a balance between protecting its business interests and meeting the public’s expectations for openness and competition.

text: A randomized, open-label trial evaluated the technique for epidural anesthesia during vaginal delivery. Thirty-one women were assigned to receive epidural analgesia either using solely the loss of resistance technique, or the same technique supplemented by epidural electric stimulation. Each epidural was first tested with 3 mL of 1% lidocaine; any sign of motor blockade at this stage resulted in the case being classified as a failure. Analgesia was considered successful if, 30 minutes after administering 10 mL of 0.22% ropivacaine with fentanyl, there was at least a 2-point reduction in pain score and bilateral loss of sensation from L1 to T10. Results showed success rates of 97% (85–100%) for the group using electric stimulation versus 77% (61–89%) for the loss of resistance group alone (P = 0.053). When only cases without detectable motor blockade at the test dose were analyzed, the success rate increased to 100% (92–100%) in the stimulation group versus 80% (63–91%) in the non-stimulation group (P = 0.024). Despite the study’s lack of blinding, small sample size, and inclusion of pilot data, the findings suggest that epidural electric stimulation may enhance the effectiveness of labor analgesia via the loss of resistance technique.

The failure rate of epidural anesthesia using the loss of resistance technique is 13–23%.

To investigate the efficacy of epidural electric stimulation-guided epidural analgesia in vaginal delivery.

An open label randomized prospective study.

Laboring women were randomized to two groups: epidural catheter insertion using only a loss of resistance technique or a loss of resistance technique with confirmation by electric stimulation. Catheters in both groups were initially tested with 3 ml of 1% lidocaine and those with any evidence of motor blockade were considered intrathecal. Sensory blockade and an 11 point numerical rating score for pain were assessed 30 minutes after administration of an epidural bolus of 10 ml of 0.22% ropivacaine with fentanyl. Successful epidural analgesia was defined as a decrease of 2 or more in the pain score and a bilateral L1-T10 sensory blockade.

Thirty-one patients were randomized to each group. The first 20 patients in each group were enrolled in a pilot study and were also included in the final analysis. One patient in the electric stimulation group was excluded owing to dural puncture by the Tuohy needle. One patient in each group demonstrated motor blockade after test dose and were considered failures. The number (% (95% confidence interval)) of successful cases were 29 out of 30 (97% (85, 100%)) in the electric stimulation group and 24 out of 31 (77% (61, 89%)) in the loss of resistance group (P = 0.053). However, analysis of only patients with absence of motor blockade revealed that 29 out of 29 (100% (92, 100%)) patients in the electric stimulation group and 24 of 29 (80% (63, 91%)) patients in the loss of resistance group had adequate analgesia (P = 0.024).

Although limited by lack of blinding, small study size and inclusion of pilot study data, this study suggests epidural electric stimulation improves the success rate of subsequent labor analgesia.
</source>

text: Over a two-year follow-up of 429 eyes implanted with intravitreal dexamethasone (IDI), the likelihood of intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation was assessed across various thresholds. At 12–24 months, approximately 50–60% of eyes reached an IOP of ≥21 mmHg, about 25–30% reached ≥25 mmHg, and roughly 6–7% exceeded ≥35 mmHg. The probability of starting IOP-lowering medications ranged from 31% to 54% during this period. Eyes with glaucoma or ocular hypertension (OHT) displayed a higher chance of mild IOP increases (≥21 mmHg; 65.1%, 75%, or 57.8% depending on the threshold), but similar rates of moderate (≥25 mmHg) and severe (≥35 mmHg) elevations were found in both glaucoma/OHT and non-glaucomatous eyes, with no significant difference between groups. Only 0.9% of eyes required glaucoma surgery. Baseline data showed 8.8% of eyes had glaucoma, 6.7% had OHT, and 16.9% were already using IOP-lowering medication. Overall, moderate IOP elevation (≥25 mmHg) was common (around 30%) and typically managed with topical treatment, while major elevations were rare and did not necessitate surgery in most cases.

<source>
To evaluate the long-term cumulative probability of intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation with the intravitreal dexamethasone implant (IDI) when used to treat different indications: diabetic macular edema, uveitis, retinal vein occlusion.

705 IDI injections (429 eyes) were assessed and Kaplan-Meier graphs were generated to assess: the probability of different levels of IOP elevation (IOP≥21, ≥25 or ≥35 mmHg), IOP change ≥10 mmHg, initiation of IOP-lowering treatment, glaucoma surgery, IOP change with repeat injections and IOP elevation in eyes with glaucoma and ocular hypertension (OHT).

The cumulative probability of IOP ≥21, ≥25 and ≥35 mmHg was 50%-60%, 25%-30% and 6%-7% at 12–24 months, respectively. The probability of initiating IOP-lowering medication was 31%-54% at 12–24 months. Glaucoma and OHT eyes had a higher probability of mild IOP elevation (≥21 mmHg, 65.1%, 75% and 57.8%, p = 0.01), yet a similar moderate (≥25 mmHg, 22.3%, 28% and 30.2%, p = 0.91) and severe elevation of IOP (≥35 mmHg, 3.7%, 7.1% and 4%, p = 0.71) as normal eyes. Glaucoma surgery was required in only 0.9% cases (4/429). At baseline, 8.8% of the treated eyes had glaucoma, 6.7% OHT and 16.9% were already on IOP-lowering medication.

In the long-term (24 months), IOP elevation is common, generally mild (30% IOP, ≥25 mmHg) and well-tolerated, resolving with topical treatment (54%) and rarely requiring surgery (0.9%).
</source>

text: Dirk Lawrence’s marriage to Martha is strained by his sudden fits of jealousy. Seeking counsel, Martha asks Ellery Queen for guidance in handling her husband’s outbursts. When she approaches, however, Dirk arrives expecting the worst and, in a fit of anger, attacks Ellery. The next day, Dirk offers a tentative explanation—he recalls a childhood trauma involving his father killing his mother’s lover, which he believes fuelled his current distrust. Ellery’s secretary and close friend, Nikki Porter, encourages Ellery to stay involved and, to keep tabs on the Lawrences, moves in with them and agrees to help as Dirk’s book editor. Nikki soon informs Ellery that Martha is holding secret meetings with Van Harrison, an attractive actor, which seem to be arranged through coded invitations sent in plain envelope that appear to be advertisements but actually bear Martha’s name and address in vivid scarlet ink. Each meeting is scheduled using a cryptic system: an envelope contains only a date, time, and a letter of the alphabet, progressing from A upward. Eventually, the pattern is uncovered by Ellery and linked to a New York city guidebook. When the sequence reaches the letter W, Dirk discovers the secret meetings and follows Martha to Van’s house in the Darien suburb. In a violent confrontation, Dirk breaks in and shoots both Van and Martha, leaving the latter for dead. As Martha lies near death, Van manages to write two letters with his own blood—first an "X," then a "Y"—on the wall before dying. Ellery must interpret these clues just as Dirk’s trial is about to end. With the help of a private audience with the judge, Ellery manages to bring justice for the crimes committed.

 Dirk and Martha Lawrence are apparently not the happiest couple in New York, despite her millions of dollars and his fairly successful mystery-writing career. Dirk apologizes the next day, telling the story of how his father had killed his mother's lover, thereby causing his over-reaction. Ellery's secretary and inamorata Nikki Porter urges him to stay involved in the situation and Nikki moves in with the Lawrences to keep an eye on things (and act as Dirk's secretary on a stalled book). The meetings are arranged with innocuous envelopes that look like advertising, but with Martha's name and address written in scarlet typewriter ink. Also, the envelopes contain only a day, time and a sequential letter of the alphabet—a code that is soon linked to a New York Guidebook. By the time the meetings have progressed from "A" through to "W", Dirk has found out about the affair and followed Martha to Van's home in the suburb of Darien. He breaks in, confronts the pair and shoots them both, seriously wounding Martha, who nearly dies. Van Harrison has just enough time before he dies to leave a dying clue—using his own blood, he writes an "X", then a "Y" on the wall, and dies. Ellery must consider the significance of this dying message and finally solves it, just as Dirk's murder trial is about to conclude. After Ellery gets a private conversation with the judge, a criminal then receives justice.

text: On a faded star map, Planet 14 appeared as little more than a dot, a remote world sheltering a battered exodus of refugees. For Belfeor, it offered swift profit—he’d only to wield iron and extract its dangerous, radioactive riches for offworld buyers. Maddalena saw it as a last test, a chance to earn her place in the Corps Galactica. Saikmar still saw his stolen homeland, a city and its people snatched by betrayal. To Gus Langenschmidt, Planet 14 was an odd assignment—monitoring the skies, quietly aiding those being subjugated, knowing any direct involvement could cost them everything. None of them truly knew each other, and that made every choice all the more dangerous.

text:
An estimated 160,000 people attended the Fringe Festival Cavalcade, an annual procession of over 3,000 marchers marking the start of the Fringe.

Festival director Gudgin advised audiences to choose their shows carefully, estimating it would take five years, eleven months, and sixteen days to see every performance back-to-back. The event is scheduled to conclude on August 28.

A recent Edinburgh City Council study found that the Fringe contributes more than £75 million to the local economy each year. Festival roles range from rickshaw drivers and show announcers to individuals shouting out details for incoming acts and cueing audiences to take their seats, as well as collecting discarded flyers.

At the Assembly venue on George Street and the 800 Assembly Hall on the Royal Mile, tickets had been sold for 97,000 by the previous Friday—exceeding the total sold in 1999. Among the performances, Danish-Egyptian comedian Omar Marzouk presented a stand-up routine addressing the Prophet Mohammed cartoon controversy.

Rev Donald Reid, representing the Festival of Spirituality and Peace, welcomed renewed attention to religious themes, attributing the surge to a growing hunger for faith and spirituality. As part of Bible Babel Live!, the complete Bible was read aloud in English, Greek, and Chinese over 80 hours across ten days.

The religious programming gained further momentum with the passage of the Racial and Religious Hatred Act in the UK, which aims to offer equal legal protection to all faiths. However, some comedians, including Rowan Atkinson, expressed concern that such legislation could stifle satire by criminalizing it.

Other notable productions included "Jesus: The Guantanamo Years," a one-man show by Abie Philbin Bowman, in which he portrays Jesus as a bearded Middle Eastern man detained at Guantanamo after confessing his readiness to die as a martyr. The venue also hosted "The Black Jew Dialogues," "According to Jesus," and "Situation Comedy," a satirical play from Israel inspired by real-life events such as suicide bombings. "Breasts and Burgers," a surreal adaptation of Guillaume Apollinaire’s work, featured the US flag torn nightly, prompting criticism from Cecile Shea, US consul to Scotland, who warned of potential offense to American audiences.

Actor Mel Smith, portraying Winston Churchill in "Allegiance," was forced to abstain from his signature cigar, as smoking in enclosed spaces has become illegal in Scotland. Despite this, the theater was threatened with closure if Smith did not comply.

Organisers are calling for increased funding, from both public and private sources, to support the continued success of the festival.

The Assembly venue, with theatres on George Street and the 800 Assembly Hall on the Royal Mile, said it had sold 97,000 tickets by last Friday - more than the entire number it sold in 1999.

Danish-Egyptian comedian Omar Marzouk performs a standup routine on the Prophet Mohammed cartoon controversy.

Rev Donald Reid, a spokesman for the Festival of Spirituality and Peace, a religious gathering that runs alongside the Fringe, welcomed the focus on religion, calling it a reflection of an upsurge in the thirst for faith and spirituality.

In Bible Babel Live! the Bible is read, in English, Greek and Chinese, from start to finish in 80 hours over 10 days .

The religious theme received further impetus from the Racial and Religious Hatred Act introduced in the UK, which sought to give all faiths equal protection, was condemned by comedians such as Rowan Atkinson who feared it would turn satire into a criminal offence.

The Black Jew Dialogues and According to Jesus were other shows on offer. The Situation Comedy is a play from Israel about a suicide bombing written and performed by Robbie Gringras. According to Gringras, it was inspired by true events, including suicide bombings in Israel.

In Breasts and Burgers, a surrealist spectacle adapted from a play by 20th-century avant-gardist Guillaume Apolliniare - the US flag is ripped apart onstage each night. Cecile Shea, the US consul in Scotland, has said the play could cause hurt to ordinary Americans.

Actor Mel Smith, who plays Winston Churchill in Allegiance had to go without lighting the trademark cigar, as smoking in an enclosed public space is now a crime in Scotland. Officials threatened to close down the theater, the Assembly Rooms, if he lit up.

Organisers of the Show have called for more funding, both from public sources as well as from private businesses, to help the show.

text: A new dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) method, combining system identification with denoising and an extended Kalman filter (EKF), is presented. The extended-Kalman-filter-based DMD (EKFDMD) is introduced as an online algorithm suitable for datasets with few degrees of freedom (DoF). However, the algorithm demands substantial computational resources for systems with many DoFs. To address this limitation, the integration of truncated proper orthogonal decomposition (trPOD) enables application of EKFDMD to high-DoF problems, despite losing full online operation. Notably, EKFDMD outperforms other methods in the presence of system noise. When coupled with trPOD—though not fully online—EKFDMD achieves strong results even for many-DoF systems, as demonstrated by a fluid mechanics example. These results underscore the improved performance of EKFDMD and its enhanced variant in system identification and denoising tasks.

text: Spasticity in stroke patients often limits functional recovery. While prior research has addressed associations between brain lesions and spasticity, the specific contributions of particular lesions remain unclear. This retrospective longitudinal study evaluated 45 stroke patients using the modified Ashworth Scale, with repeated assessments at 0 (within two weeks of stroke), 1, 3, and 6 months. Brain anatomy was analyzed via voxel-based lesion symptom mapping (VLSM) on MRI images. The results indicated that most patients with spasticity exhibited increased spasticity within three months post-stroke. VLSM revealed that lesions in the superior corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, posterior corona radiata, thalamus, putamen, premotor cortex, and insula were linked with upper-limb spasticity, while lesions in the superior corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, posterior corona radiata, thalamus, putamen, and external capsule were related to lower-limb spasticity. These findings suggest that specific white matter tracts and subcortical structures play a role in spasticity development after stroke. Such insights may inform more targeted rehabilitation plans and deepen understanding of spasticity's neuroanatomical basis.

Spasticity is an important barrier that can hinder the restoration of function in stroke patients. Although several studies have attempted to elucidate the relationship between brain lesions and spasticity, the effects of specific brain lesions on the development of spasticity remain unclear. Thus, the present study investigated the effects of stroke lesions on spasticity in stroke patients. The present retrospective longitudinal observational study assessed 45 stroke patients using the modified Ashworth Scale to measure muscle spasticity. Each patient was assessed four times: initially (within 2 weeks of stroke) and at 1, 3, and 6 months after the onset of stroke. Brain lesions were analyzed using voxel-based lesion symptom mapping (VLSM) with magnetic resonance imaging images. Spasticity developed to a certain degree within 3 months in most stroke patients with spasticity. The VLSM method with non-parametric mapping revealed that lesions in the superior corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, posterior corona radiata, thalamus, putamen, premotor cortex, and insula were associated with the development of upper-limb spasticity. Additionally, lesions of the superior corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, posterior corona radiata, thalamus, putamen, and external capsule were associated with the development of lower-limb spasticity. The present study identified several brain lesions that contributed to post-stroke spasticity. Specifically, the involvement of white matter tracts and the striatum influenced the development of spasticity in the upper and lower limbs of stroke patients. These results may be useful for planning rehabilitation strategies and for understanding the pathophysiology of spasticity in stroke patients.
</source>

text:
Risky sexual behaviors are linked to the spread of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and unintended pregnancies—major health challenges for youth globally. This review evaluates the effectiveness of narrated mass media programs in encouraging safer sexual behaviors among young people in both developed and developing countries.

We conducted electronic and manual searches to identify randomized and quasi-experimental studies with strong counterfactual designs, published from 1985 through the first quarter of 2017. Meta-analyses were performed using mixed-effects models to estimate overall effects.

Ten studies met our criteria—eight experimental and two quasi-experimental—encompassing a total of 23,476 participants (median study size: 902). The interventions employed entertainment education narratives.

These programs showed small but significant effects on three sexual behaviors: reducing the number of sexual partners (SMD 0.17, 95% CI 0.02–0.33), decreasing unprotected sex (SMD 0.08, 95% CI 0.03–0.12), and increasing the uptake of STI testing and management (SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.11–0.46). Effects were not observed in reducing intergenerational sex (SMD 0.06, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.19). While knowledge about sexual health improved with moderate effects (SMD 0.67, 95% CI 0.32–1.02), no significant changes were found in attitudes.

While these entertainment-based media programs produced modest but real benefits in promoting safer sex, their scalability is supported by cost efficiencies compared to face-to-face approaches. The use of general youth populations and the predominance of effectiveness trials address concerns about broader applicability. Nonetheless, the limited number of high-quality studies highlights the need for more rigorous research. Future studies should explore how different subgroups and intervention features moderate these effects.

This review studies the effectiveness of narrated mass media programs in promoting safer sexual practices among youth in developed and developing countries.

Entertainment education had medium-size effects on knowledge outcomes (SMD = 0.67, 95% CI = 0.32–1.02, seven effect sizes), where a time-decay relationship is observed. No effects were found on attitudes.

Although mass media entertainment had small effects in promoting safer sexual practices, its economies of scales over face-to-face interventions suggest its potential to be a cost-effective tool above an audience threshold. The use of study participants from the general youth population and the use of mostly effectiveness trials mitigate concerns regarding its scalability. The overall paucity of high-quality studies affirms the need for strengthening the evidence base of entertainment education. Future research should be undertaken to understand the moderator effects for different subgroups and intervention characteristics.
</source>

text: A standardized suicide screening instrument has not yet been developed for the Malaysian context, even as suicide rates rise nationally and internationally. This study seeks to create the first Malay-language adaptation of a suicide screening tool tailored to Malaysia’s diverse and multicultural population. The research was conducted in three sequential phases. Initially, items were selected from established suicide ideation and attitude scales. In the pilot phase, the questionnaire was refined for the Yatt Suicide Attitude Scale (YSAS) within the local context. The final validation involved 219 university students, with the original 16-item instrument reduced after factor analysis to a 10-item version comprising two factors: Suicide Ideation and Suicide Attempt, each with five items. Both factors demonstrated strong internal reliability (Cronbach’s alpha of 0.89 and 0.86), explaining 68.4% of the variance. Despite suicide rate becoming a growing trend in research locally and globally, there is no standard measuring instrument developed in Malaysia. The aim of this study is to establish the first ever Malay version of suicide screening tool that is suitable and fit with multiracial and complex culture of Malaysia.

This study comprises of three phases, namely (1) items selection phase, (2) pilot study phase, and (3) scale validation phase. During the first phase, the items were selected from items pools which gathered from previous suicide ideation/ attitude scales. Then the pilot study was carried out to examine the items for Yatt Suicide Attitude Scale (YSAS). Lastly, the Yatt Suicide Attitude Scale (YSAS) validation study was conducted with 219 university students.

Initial version of YSAS comprised 16 items and three components. After factor analysis, the questionnaire was reduced into only two components (Suicide Ideation and Suicide Attempt) with 5 items each. Both of the components obtained high reliability value (.89 and.86 respectively) and the questionnaire accounted for 67.84% of the total variance.

The analysis showed that YSAS has an acceptable reliability and validity for Malaysian population. Although these findings corroborate literature on development of suicide ideation assessment instrument for specific cultural context, there is a need to further examine its reliability with clinical population and general population of different cultural context in Malaysia.
</source>

text: There is growing evidence that developing handwriting skills is linked to better academic achievement. This developmental process starts in kindergarten, when children’s writing closely resembles drawing—mostly scribbles. It takes several years before children write competently. Research indicates that motor practice is vital in shaping the mental representations of letters, though the specific relationship between handwriting proficiency and teaching methods remains less understood. This study examined the impact of cursive writing instruction in first-grade classrooms. The sample included 141 typically developing students without cognitive, sensory, or significant motor disorders. The intervention involved teaching all letter rules and characteristics through demonstration of correct writing movements, emphasizing letter connections to form words. A magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck Indonesia’s Yogyakarta and Central Java region early Saturday morning, killing at least 5,427 people and injuring thousands. Severe damage was reported in Yogyakarta, with over 3,000 buildings collapsed and essential infrastructure, including electricity and communications, disrupted. According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the quake occurred at 5:54 a.m. local time (22:54 UTC Friday), with its epicenter roughly 25 km southwest of Yogyakarta.

Just before the quake, Mount Merapi—a volcano that has shown heightened activity in recent weeks—released a large plume of purple smoke and ash. Volcanologists have noted that the earthquake intensified Merapi’s activity further, adding to the immediate dangers in the region. Indonesia, situated on the Pacific Ring of Fire, is among the world’s most earthquake- and volcano-prone areas, and the event is expected to compound existing risks.

Rescue and recovery efforts have been complicated by continued aftershocks; the USGS reports aftershocks up to magnitude 4.8. Hospitals are struggling due to limited medical supplies, staff shortages, and the ongoing tremors. The Yogyakarta airport runway was damaged, forcing its closure until at least Sunday, complicating emergency evacuations and relief deliveries.

In response to the disaster, several countries have pledged assistance. The UK has offered £3 million ($5.6 million), Australia has donated A$3 million ($2.27 million), China has contributed $2 million, and further support has come from the United States, the European Union, Japan, and UNICEF. Organizations such as the Red Cross, Red Crescent, OXFAM, and UNICEF are already distributing emergency tents and supplies to affected communities.

Many residents were forced to spend the night outdoors, either fearing further aftershocks or having already lost their homes. In the Bantul district, nearly 80% of homes were destroyed, leaving an estimated 150,000 people homeless. President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has visited the area and has ordered the deployment of the army to aid in the rescue and recovery operations.

text: Legal systems unfold in ways that mirror the tangled patterns seen in ecosystems, economies, and social institutions, yet their inner complexity has rarely been mapped with precision. This study builds a network model using links between constitutional provisions and actual court rulings, turning abstract legal doctrine into a tangible structure. The resulting networks aren’t uniform—some nodes carry heavy weight, others remain peripheral—reflecting a heterogeneity common in complex systems. By comparing legal networks across different political regimes, we track how changes in society alter their shape. A core of foundational legal connections holds steady across all systems, resisting shifts in governance or culture. But beyond this stable center, the arrangement of links diverges sharply between regimes. These variations aren’t random; they align with differences in institutional design and social conditions. While the basic architecture of law endures, the way its elements interlock changes in measurable ways. The approach offers a way to read legal systems not as rigid codes, but as dynamic structures shaped by real-world pressures. It opens pathways for evaluating legal change, testing policy impacts, and understanding how law adapts—without claiming to predict its course.

text:
This study examined survival outcomes for Polish women with cervical cancer (CC) and their adherence to established treatment protocols. Poland’s CC mortality rate remains 70% above the EU average, despite national guidelines aligning with those of the European Society of Gynaecological Oncology (ESGO) and international standards. We investigated whether gaps in treatment implementation might explain this disparity.

Using a retrospective multicenter design, we analyzed medical records from 1,247 women who completed at least two years of follow-up. Among those with FIGO IB to IVA disease—where concurrent chemoradiotherapy is the standard of care in well-resourced settings—fewer Polish patients received chemotherapy compared to countries with better overall survival. This gap persisted even though treatment protocols were formally in line with global recommendations.

For FIGO IA to IIA cases, treatment patterns matched those recommended by the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), suggesting that care for earlier-stage disease follows established best practices. Yet, the inconsistency in chemotherapy use for more advanced stages, combined with known limitations in Poland’s cervical cancer screening program, points to systemic challenges in care delivery. These findings indicate that adherence to treatment protocols alone does not ensure improved outcomes, and that broader structural factors likely affect survival among Polish women with CC.

In the late 1700s, Lestat de Lioncourt, born to a minor noble family in rural France, flees with his childhood friend Nicolas de Lenfent—known as Nicki—to Paris. Soon after, he is captured by Magnus, a rogue vampire who kills Lestat’s mother, Gabrielle, on the same night. In her final moments, Gabrielle clutches Lestat and speaks words he cannot fully hear. He bites her in a desperate attempt to preserve her, and she becomes his first companion. He cuts ties with Nicki out of fear, leaving him behind without warning.

Years later, Nicki is taken by Armand, who turns him into a vampire. The bond between them frays quickly; Nicki retreats into a silence that grows heavier with time. Eventually, he walks into a fire and dies, not in battle or violence, but in quiet surrender to sorrow.

Armand later tells Lestat he was made by Marius, an ancient vampire who has endured centuries. Driven by this revelation, Lestat travels across Europe and North Africa, carving symbols into stone as signs of his search. He journeys with Gabrielle until she abandons him in Egypt. There, exposed to sunlight, he burns and sinks into the earth to sleep.

He is found and revived by Marius, who brings him to an island in the Mediterranean. There, Marius shows him Akasha and Enkil, two ancient vampires imprisoned beneath the surface. Marius warns him not to return to them. After Marius leaves on a short absence, Lestat takes Nicki’s old violin and plays in the chamber beneath the villa. Akasha drinks from him. He drinks from her in return. Enkil, furious at the violation of the old order, nearly kills him. Marius arrives in time to save him, expels him from the island.

The story ends with Lestat standing before an audience in San Francisco, about to perform. The moment marks a turning point—just before the events of *The Queen of the Damned* begin.

text: Along Japan’s Oga Peninsula, rising ocean temperatures have allowed Heliocidaris crassispina to expand northward, displacing Mesocentrotus nudus in the process. A 2014 survey in Toga Bay collected 106 H. crassispina individuals, revealing growth rates significantly slower than in its core range. Gonad development was assessed through size, color (measured via lightness L* and yellowness b*), and maturity. Males consistently lagged behind females in gonad development, and testicular acini maturity varied widely across individuals, indicating asynchronous spawning. The population included seven year-classes, spanning 2006 to 2012, demonstrating continuous recruitment into the new habitat. Summer temperature records from the region align with the shift, confirming warming as the primary driver. Despite successful range expansion, northern populations show reduced growth and reproductive asynchrony compared to central populations, suggesting a partial adaptation to new conditions rather than full physiological equivalence.

text: Forty-one9 Mycoplasma pneumoniae isolates from Osaka, Japan, spanning 2011 to 2017, were examined. Macrolide-resistant (MRMP) strains dominated in 2011 and 2014, detected at 71.4% to 81.8%. After 2015, resistance dropped sharply, with prevalence below 50% in subsequent years. The p1 gene genotyping showed MRMP strains mostly carried type 1. In contrast, macrolide-susceptible (MSMP) strains were predominantly type 2 or its variants. p1 genotype strongly correlated with the presence of macrolide-resistance mutations. Three isolates displayed unusual p1 PCR-RFLP patterns: two were new variants (2f, 2g), and one had a large deletion in the p1 operon. The shift in MRMP incidence after 2015 likely reflects an increase in p1 type 2 lineages, suggesting this genotype may carry a fitness cost under selective pressure from macrolides.

text:
Ecuador defeated Costa Rica 3-0 at the AOL Arena in Hamburg on Thursday, securing advancement to the knockout stage of the World Cup alongside Germany. Both teams finished Group A with six points after two matches, though Ecuador’s victory was decisive.

The match unfolded under the steady hand of Ecuador’s Colombian coach, Luis Suarez, who made strategic decisions to rest key players. Carlos Tenorio, the top scorer, and playmaker Luis Valencia were withdrawn before full time, along with central defender Giovanny Espinoza. Their absence did not disrupt Ecuador’s rhythm.

From the outset, Ecuador dictated the pace. They retained possession consistently, threading passes through midfield with precision. Costa Rica, managed by Alexandre Guimaraes, lacked cohesion in midfield and failed to generate sustained pressure against Ecuador’s goalkeeper, Christian Mora.

Ecuador scored in the seventh minute. Luis Valencia, operating from the right flank, delivered a precise cross into the penalty area. Carlos Tenorio, unmarked in front of goal, powered a header past Costa Rican keeper Jose Porras.

Despite several opportunities in the first half, neither side converted. Douglas Sequeira missed a free header at the far post. Edison Mendez and Agustin Delgado came close, with the latter’s attempt skimming wide. Delgado found the net shortly after, driving a low shot from inside the box that nestled into the near corner.

After the break, Tenorio’s replacement, Kaviedes, was involved in a sequence that culminated in a goal. A save from Porras was followed by a misfired header, but Kaviedes turned and struck a curling volley from the far post, finishing off another Mendez cross.

Costa Rica had a moment of near-miss when Alvaro Saborio’s chip struck the upright. Two long-range attempts—by Carlos Hernandez and Mauricio Solis—were notable but lacked accuracy. Ecuador’s defense, disciplined and alert, kept a clean sheet, marking their second consecutive shutout in the tournament.

Ecuador now faces Germany on June 20 to determine the group’s top seed.

Dairine, Nita’s younger sister, finds Nita’s wizard’s manual tucked in a drawer and begins reading it. Without warning, she swears the Wizard’s Oath in her own name. The ritual grants her a personal manual and a portable computer she calls Spot. She uses it to ride a worldgate to Mars, then to the Crossings—where she’s ambushed by agents of the Lone Power. She escapes through a barred gate into a bar on a world where light bends at sharp angles. A man in a coat lined with dead stars helps her through. They vanish through a gate into a planet made of solidified silicon, the size of a moon.

When she wakes, she’s standing inside a machine so large it fills the sky. She starts building mobiles—small, shifting shapes that move on their own, shaped like old software icons, old game avatars, a Jedi, a droid from a film she once saw. The planet responds to her mind, generating quicklife. But one mobile turns sharp, its surface flickering with dark logic. It attacks her.

Nita and Kit, who’ve been tracking Dairine’s absence since her signal died near the Crossings, arrive via a forgotten gate. They bring Peach, a macaw with cracked irises and a voice like static—she reveals she’s the One’s Champion. They fight the mobile, and Peach uses a word that halts the expansion of spacetime itself. The resulting burst of light erases the Lone Power from existence. He vanishes, returning to the source of all power, leaving only a warning: destroy what’s left of his shadow.

The universe keeps growing. They return. Dairine’s computer, now with articulated limbs, walks behind her as she climbs the stairs. Nita and Kit tell their parents what happened, not in awe, not in fear, just as it happened.

At thirty-two, Elizabeth Gilbert had the life most people would call successful: a house, a husband, a name in print. But she woke each morning with an emptiness that no accomplishment could fill. Her marriage had frayed into silence, and she spent nights on the bathroom floor, not from illness, but from a quiet, unrelenting ache. The divorce came slowly, mired in legal disputes, and in the pause between separation and finality, she began another relationship—hasty, desperate, and over before the year turned. She was left alone, raw, and afraid.

While writing about yoga retreats in Bali, she met a Balinese healer, a man whose family had practiced medicine for generations. He said she would return. She believed him.

After the divorce was settled, she used the advance from her book to leave. She spent four months in Italy, eating slowly, watching light fall across stone, learning that joy didn’t have to be earned. Then three months in India, sitting in silence, trying to still the noise in her head. The final stretch was in Bali, not for answers, but for balance. She didn’t find enlightenment. She found a man—Brazilian, from a factory in the highlands, quiet, steady. They began to talk. That was when she stopped waiting for something to happen. She started living.

Bruce Drexel returns to Provence after learning of Piers’s suicide. His wife Sylvie has been institutionalized for months, and the weight of their shared past presses hard on him during the visit to Avignon with Toby. He arranges the funeral, moves through the rituals with mechanical precision, and drifts into memories of winter nights when the three of them—Piers, Sylvie, and Bruce—were bound by a love that felt absolute. A novel by Robin Sutcliffe, written in the aftermath, offers a version of those days, but its truth remains unclear.

The next section, "Macabru," shifts to Egypt. Bruce, Piers, and Sylvie travel across the desert, drawn by Akkad, a man who speaks in half-remembered phrases and claims to know a Gnostic sect. They follow him to a desolate place named Macabru, where the rituals unfold in silence and sunlight. The Nile journey here anticipates a later passage on the Rhine, not as echo but as repetition of a pattern—something that repeats, not because it must, but because it did.

Then comes "Sutcliffe, or the Venetian Documents," narrated by Sutcliffe himself. He is in Venice, estranged from Pia, Bruce’s sister, and burdened by a marriage that failed before it could begin. His account deepens the ambiguity: was any of it real? The narrative slips between recollection and invention.

Back in Avignon, Bruce and Toby discuss the Knights Templar, not as history but as a kind of cipher for what they’ve seen—the idea that truth might be encrypted in ritual. The conversation breaks when a new fragment surfaces: "The Green Notebook." It’s a raw draft, full of sketches and half-sentences, dating before the novel’s final form.

The last section, "Dinner at Quartilla’s," brings Blanford, who writes about Sutcliffe as a character. He dines with the elderly Duchess Tu, who died years ago. She speaks, but her voice is not her own.

The novel ends without a closing sentence. Instead, an Envoi traces the lineages: not through birth, but through what has been written, remembered, or claimed.

text: A summit of global powers unfolds in Baghdad, though news of it leaks into public view. Unseen, a clandestine extremist group plots to sabotage the gathering. Victoria Jones, a young woman traveling through the region, stumbles upon the body of a British agent—Henry "Fakir" Carmichael—collapsed in her hotel room. His last words, spoken in a fading breath, name three fragments: "Lucifer," "Basrah," and "Lefarge." She deciphers them carefully. "Lucifer" refers to Edward, a man she believed to be her lover, now revealed as the architect of the conspiracy. "Basrah" names the city where key documents were disseminated. "Lefarge" is not a name but a misheard echo of "Defarge"—a character from Dickens’s *A Tale of Two Cities*, suggesting the documents might be hidden in a location tied to that narrative. The reference calls to mind Christie’s earlier novel, *The Man in the Brown Suit*, which followed a romantic plotline with a mysterious, appealing man who becomes the heroine’s partner. In this case, a similarly enigmatic man surfaces in Victoria’s path, but he does not survive. The narrative does not end with romantic entanglement. Instead, it shifts to an archaeologist—calm, reserved, grounded—whose involvement with Victoria feels deliberate, not accidental. At this stage of her life, Christie was married to Max Mallowan, and her fiction reflects a quieter, more measured emotional arc.

text: After two years of follow-up in 429 eyes with intravitreal dexamethasone implants (IDI), intraocular pressure (IOP) changes were analyzed across established thresholds. By 12 to 24 months, roughly half the eyes reached IOP ≥21 mmHg, a quarter reached ≥25 mmHg, and about 6–7% exceeded 35 mmHg. The proportion requiring IOP-lowering medications ranged from 31% to 54%. Eyes with pre-existing glaucoma or ocular hypertension (OHT) showed higher rates of mild IOP rise (≥21 mmHg: 57.8% to 75%), but moderate (≥25 mmHg) and severe (≥35 mmHg) elevations occurred at similar frequencies in both glaucomatous/OHT and non-glaucomatous eyes, with no statistically significant difference. Surgery for glaucoma was needed in only 0.9% of cases. At baseline, 8.8% of eyes had glaucoma, 6.7% had OHT, and 16.9% were already on IOP-lowering treatment. Moderate IOP elevation (≥25 mmHg) was common—occurring in about 30% of cases—and was usually controlled with topical agents, while major elevations remained uncommon and seldom required surgical intervention.

text: In 1943, amid the upheaval of war in Palestine, a group of Jewish children who had fled the Soviet Union began to speak. Their accounts, recorded by the Eastern Center for Information—a unit of the Polish government—documented their experiences before, during, and after the war. These testimonies, later compiled by Grynberg, form the core of *The Children of Zion*, published in January 1998. The children described the moment the Germans and Russians arrived, the abrupt end of normal life, and their long, dangerous journeys across Eastern Europe. They spoke of life in labor camps, of displacement, and of the Sikorsky Agreement, which finally permitted their exit. Many had lost parents; nearly all had endured separation, fear, and survival in isolation. Their voices, raw and unvarnished, detail the fragmentation of childhood under siege. Now archived at the Hoover Institution, Stanford University, these interviews are not a narrative shaped for public consumption but a direct record—preserved not as a monument, but as a refusal to let the past dissolve into silence.

text:
Ecuador defeated Poland 2-0 in their second Group A fixture at the World Cup, the result sealed by a disciplined defensive stand and two clinical goals. The game unfolded at the Veltins-Arena in Gelsenkirchen, where a large contingent of Polish supporters watched their side fail to generate consistent pressure.

The opening twenty minutes offered little in the way of clear chances. Ecuador struck first in the 28th minute when Carlos Tenario rose at the far post to meet a right-sided throw-in, driving the ball low into the corner past goalkeeper Artur Boruc. Ivan Hurtado, Ecuador’s captain and central defender, anchored the backline through the first half; he was withdrawn in the 67th minute due to a hamstring strain sustained in a late tackle.

Poland increased their share of possession after halftime, but their attacks stalled repeatedly in the final third. Passes were inconsistent, and the midfield failed to connect with the forwards. Ecuador absorbed pressure, relying on quick transitions and tight positioning. Their second goal came in the 80th minute, following a loose clearance from a Polish defender. The ball fell to an Ecuadorian attacker, who advanced into a two-on-one, and despite Boruc’s dive, the finish was placed firmly into the net.

In the final five minutes, Poland found their rhythm briefly. Two shots came close—both striking the crossbar and post—before being saved by goalkeeper Christian Mora. The late flurry did not alter the outcome. Ecuador’s backline, led by Giovanny Espinoza and the injured Hurtado, held firm. Ecuador’s next opponent is Costa Rica; Poland must now face Germany, who won their opening match on Friday.

text: A longitudinal retrospective study tracked 45 stroke patients to examine how brain lesions correlated with the onset of muscle spasticity. Spasticity in the upper limbs was assessed using the modified Ashworth Scale at four intervals: shortly after stroke, and again at 1, 3, and 6 months. Brain lesions were mapped via voxel-based lesion symptom mapping (VLSM) using MRI data. Most patients developed detectable spasticity within three months of stroke. Lesions in the superior and posterior corona radiata, internal capsule, thalamus, putamen, premotor cortex, and insula were consistently associated with upper-limb spasticity. For lower-limb involvement, damage in the superior and posterior corona radiata, caudate nucleus, thalamus, putamen, and external capsule predicted spasticity. These results pinpoint specific white matter and subcortical regions whose disruption underlies post-stroke spasticity. The findings clarify the neuroanatomical roots of spasticity, offering a foundation for refining rehabilitation strategies and guiding future research into its physiological mechanisms.

In Kenya, researchers tested whether mobile phone-based computer-assisted interviews could reliably collect nutrition data in a region where undernutrition persists at high levels, often worsened by drought and conflict. The study focused on two indicators: the Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women (MDD-W) and the Minimum Acceptable Diet for infants and young children (MAD). Over a week, they conducted test-retest interviews with 1,821 households using both mobile phone calls and traditional face-to-face surveys.

The mobile method reached 75% of surveyed individuals. Women reported similar dietary diversity across both formats. But children’s outcomes differed. When assessed via phone, children showed higher dietary diversity—on average, 0.45 more food groups (95% CI: 0.34–0.56)—and 0.75 more meals per day (95% CI: 0.53–0.96) compared to in-person interviews. These shifts led to a 17% higher estimate of children receiving adequate diets under the CATI method. 

Mobile coverage gaps were small—1% to 7%—and mostly affected households headed by younger women with lower incomes. These were not random omissions, but tied to socioeconomic patterns already known to correlate with limited access to communication devices.

The results point to a measurable upward bias in mobile phone surveys for child nutrition metrics. While not uniform across all indicators, the effect was clear: CATI surveys tended to report higher levels of dietary adequacy than face-to-face interviews. The difference ranged from no change to a 25% increase in the proportion of children meeting dietary standards. This suggests that using mobile phone data alone may overestimate progress on child nutrition, particularly in settings like Kenya. Interpretation must account for this systematic difference.

One week after Danse Macabre, Anita and Jean-Claude are still reeling when enforcers from the Vampire Council arrive. Under their influence, Richard and Jean-Claude nearly kill each other. The Harlequin claims to uphold vampire law, but its actions contradict its own code, making it liable to formal retaliation. Edward doesn’t kill any of them. Instead, in trying to break a psychic tracking spell the Harlequin placed on her and Jean-Claude, Anita forms a psychic link that allows her to end a life. The human servant of one vampire dies shortly after—not by her hand, but as a result of the connection she established. They recover and confront the remaining members at Malcolm’s Church of Eternal Life. They win not only in combat but in truth: the Harlequin had not acted under Council authority, but was planning to seize Jean-Claude’s territory.

Afterward, Anita fights her anger, barely holding back the Mother of All Darkness from taking form. She abandons her former allies, the werelions, to die. With many of her allies wounded, Rex Joseph, the werelion, is asked to surrender to sexual demand so Anita can regain strength. He refuses—citing his marriage and his vow of faithfulness. In that moment, she sees his refusal not as courage, but as a betrayal of their alliance. She makes no further effort to save him.

FIFA has suspended El Salvador from international football after the government blocked the appointment of officials chosen by FIFA. The Salvadorian Football Association (FESFUT) is under sanction because President Mauricio Funes refused to accept a FIFA-appointed commission tasked with reforming the association's finances. This followed the resignation of FESFUT's president, Rodrigo Calvo, last year. Despite FIFA's efforts to restore internal governance, the government's refusal to recognize the commission qualifies as interference under FIFA regulations.

Simon "Widgie" and Jen Widgeon take a shortcut near their flat, following a path so overgrown it might have been erased by time. They don’t notice the archway at first—just a shadowed gap in the tunnel wall, half-collapsed, barely wider than a shoulder. They step through without hesitation and find themselves on a platform that looks like it hasn’t seen a train in decades, but still functions: the tracks are clear, the signals flicker, and the air carries the weight of oil, damp wood, and old iron. No one speaks. The silence is not empty—it’s full, like breath held.

Jen hears it first: a low thrum, not from the walls, but from somewhere beneath. She walks forward. Her shoes click on the concrete. Then figures appear—men in threadbare uniforms, their faces sharp under dim lamps. They grab Widgie before he can react.

Meanwhile, Jen finds a canal, narrow and pitch-black, its surface like glass. A steamboat glides across it, its hull blackened by soot, its deck empty except for three figures in oilskin coats. They don’t speak. They bind her wrists with a rope that feels too new for the place.

The truth settles: this isn’t a mistake. This is a system. Beneath North London, two groups have maintained separate networks for generations—the Railway, who keep the rails running, and the Canallers, who move through the waterways. They’ve never met openly. Now, the arrival of two strangers has ruptured the balance.

When Widgie breaks free, he runs not toward safety but toward the sound of Jen’s footsteps, toward the edge of the network. They pass through a warped junction and into the Post Office Railway—abandoned, half-collapsed, its old carriages still rusting in the dark. The moment they enter, the system fractures.

The side tunnel behind them gives way. Something long sealed beneath the earth bursts through—rats, large as hounds, their eyes blind to light, their teeth gnashing in darkness. The network shakes. The rails warp. The lights die one by one. They keep running, not knowing if they’re escaping or already inside something worse.

Still, the limited number of high-quality trials indicates a need for more targeted research to identify which program features and demographic groups respond best.

This analysis examines how social and demographic factors shape women’s control over reproductive health choices across 27 sub-Saharan African countries. Data from Demographic and Health Surveys collected between 2010 and 2016 were used to assess decision-making power in sexual and reproductive matters using binary and multivariate logistic regression.

The capacity to negotiate condom use varied widely, from 16.6% in Mali to 93.4% in Namibia. Refusal of sex followed a similar pattern, ranging from 18.3% in Mali to 92.4% in Namibia. Half of the surveyed women could request condom use, 60% could refuse sex, and 70% could make at least one reproductive health decision independently.

Women in rural areas were significantly less likely to have agency—odds ratio 0.51 (95% CI 0.48–0.54). Those without formal education had even lower odds, at 0.11 (95% CI 0.10–0.12). Muslim women were less likely to decide on reproductive matters (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.27–0.31). Unemployed women had OR 0.53 (95% CI 0.51–0.56). When a woman’s partner had no education, her chance of influencing reproductive decisions dropped sharply, to OR 0.17 (95% CI 0.16–0.19).

Factors such as residence, age, education, religion, employment status, and partner’s education were consistently linked to decision-making on sexual intercourse, condom use, and overall reproductive health choices. The results highlight structural barriers that limit autonomy. Addressing these factors offers a path toward more informed and self-directed reproductive health outcomes, particularly in marginalized communities.

text:
After leaving the church, Judd Thompson and Vicki Byrne head to O’Hare International Airport to get Judd’s car. A taxi driver, smiling and speaking softly, drops them off three miles from the terminal. As they step out into the gray light of dawn, they say a prayer together—just a few words, not much more than a breath. The moment settles between them, not grand, not ritualized, but real. They begin to see each other not as strangers who happened to walk out the same door, but as people who now carry something alike.

The parking lot is packed. They wait nearly an hour before the car is finally freed, engine grumbling to life at four in the morning. Vicki asks Judd to take her to her trailer, somewhere near the edge of the city. But when they arrive, nothing remains. The structure is gone, reduced to blackened steel and ash. No one else would know how the fire started. She stands in the empty pad, hands at her sides, and says only, “I don’t have anywhere else.”

Judd lets her stay at his apartment.

Meanwhile, Lionel finds Ryan standing in the cold, outside his house, face tight with something that isn’t anger, not exactly—more like disbelief. Ryan had left the church after learning his parents were dead. Lionel doesn’t say much. He just offers his jacket and walks with him. They go to Ryan’s house. They set up a tent in the yard, using a tarp and two folding chairs.

Later, they drive to Lionel’s place to gather clothes. On the way, his phone rings. It’s his uncle Andre—his voice thin, almost flat. He says he’s sorry for what he’s done, and that he’s ending it. Lionel calls Ryan, and they leave immediately, driving to the hotel where Andre had stayed. They arrive too late. The staff won’t confirm anything, but the body bag is already gone. No name on it.

That night, all four of them end up at Ryan’s house, huddled under the tent. No one sleeps. They don’t talk much. The next morning, Ryan insists on moving into his own place. He tells Judd he needs to try. But when they get there, the house is full of strangers—people who knew Andre, who still talk to his name like he might walk in. Ryan grabs his backpack, a change of clothes, and leaves.

They find each other again at the church. No one says much. They just share what they’ve lost, and what they’re afraid of. In the end, Lionel and Ryan decide they’ll stay with Judd and Vicki. Not because they’re safe there. But because they’ve learned, in silence, that staying together is the only thing that still makes sense.

text: Saccadic adaptation is typically assumed to occur unconsciously, as an automatic process. This study examined whether individuals can consciously suppress this adaptation, specifically whether they can actively prevent changes in saccade gain. Participants executed saccades in a double-step task: a target appeared briefly in a peripheral location, then shifted during the movement to a new position. In one condition, they were told to follow the step and fixate the final location—this promoted adaptation. In the other, they were instructed to resist adjusting their saccade, instead keeping their gaze fixed on the original target. Two experiments were run, varying the size of the target shift. For outward steps (away from the initial target), inhibition successfully suppressed gain change, resulting in near-zero adaptation. But for inward steps (toward the initial target), a small but measurable adaptation remained despite instructions to stop it. Saccade latency did not differ between conditions during inward steps. However, for outward steps, latencies were significantly longer under inhibition than during the adaptation condition. These results indicate that volitional control can reduce saccadic adaptation, especially when the target moves away from the initial goal. The persistence of adaptation during inward steps suggests that control is limited during target remapping, particularly when the new target location contradicts the original movement plan.

text: Among HIV-positive adults on antiretroviral therapy (ART) aged 18 and older, gender shapes experiences of food insecurity in ways that vary by economic context. Data from seventeen studies involving over five thousand individuals show a consistent link between being female and higher odds of food insecurity. Women in these studies had a 53% greater likelihood of facing food insecurity than men (odds ratio [OR] = 1.53, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.29 to 1.83), a difference that holds across both high-income and low- and middle-income settings. The effect is stronger in resource-limited environments, where findings from low- and middle-income countries suggest a more pronounced disparity. This pattern persists even though earlier research did not always confirm a gendered difference. The disparity likely stems from structural constraints—women often have less authority over household finances and face greater difficulty in securing food for themselves and their dependents. While some studies previously failed to detect a gender effect, the current body of evidence makes it clear that gender matters in this population. Interventions targeting food insecurity among people on ART must account for these differences. Programs cannot rely on one-size-fits-all models. Effective responses must be grounded in local realities and designed to address the specific social and economic barriers women face, including limited control over resources and unequal access to food within the household.

text: Protest responses in contingent valuation surveys appear in about one in five cases, on average, across multiple studies. This paper examines why people respond this way and assesses how including or excluding these responses affects estimates of willingness to pay (WTP) for farm animal welfare. The literature lacks clear standards: definitions of protest bids vary, motivations are poorly mapped, and most surveys ask only those who give a zero WTP for reasons. We analyze data from a survey of 1,335 people about farm animal welfare, using two distinct definitions of protest responses and conducting a full debriefing with every participant to understand their reasoning. The findings show protest bids are not signs of disengagement, nor are they driven by confusion or irrationality. A significant number of respondents cite moral judgment as their primary motivation. Importantly, not all protests result in zero WTP: only 8% of those identifying as protesting reported a zero valuation, even though they made up 32% of the protest group. Among all zero bids, just 0.4% reflect a genuine statement of satisfaction with current conditions. These results suggest excluding protest respondents introduces bias, especially since true zero WTP is extremely rare. We also produce adjusted WTP estimates by iteratively including and excluding different protest categories and outlier observations, offering a more accurate foundation for policy decisions on animal welfare valuation.

High-frequency sound (HSS) technology relies on ultrasound—frequencies above 20 kilohertz, beyond human hearing. Unlike audible sound, which disperses and fades in all directions, these inaudible waves remain tightly focused. A beam of such sound can travel up to 500 yards and concentrate on a single person. That individual perceives the sound as originating inside their head, while those nearby hear nothing. The effect enables targeted communication: a public announcement, a directional warning, or an ad delivered only to one listener. In a crowded room, one person could hear a news update while another listens to a different audio stream, with no interference. The same principle might support non-lethal crowd control. A sustained burst of HSS can disorient or immobilize, offering law enforcement or military units a tool that avoids lethal force.

Meanwhile, a new personal aircraft is nearing release. The AirScooter™, a compact, single-pilot vehicle, will go on sale later this year with a base price under $50,000. It weighs under 300 pounds and carries a total load of 350 pounds. Power comes from standard gasoline, not aviation-grade fuel. Its 5-gallon fuel tank supports two hours of flight at 55 miles per hour, with a maximum altitude of 10,000 feet. No pilot’s license is required—its design keeps it under regulatory thresholds for ultralight aircraft. The core innovation lies in the AeroTwin 4-stroke engine, developed by Pearson Motor Co. in New Zealand. Originally designed for motorcycle racing, this engine uses dual rotors on a single shaft, spinning in opposite directions. That counteracts torque, making a tail rotor unnecessary. Control is handled through a handlebar reminiscent of a motorcycle. Twisting the bars alters direction, pulling back adjusts altitude, and moving them side to side steers the vehicle, including reverse motion. Visual details and flight demonstrations are posted on AirScooter.com.

The AirScooter’s creator, Glenn Norris, is a self-taught inventor. He left formal education after third grade but has spent over three decades designing devices, starting with audio systems at age eight. Now 63 and father to eleven children, Norris intends to use any prize money to found a support group for independent inventors who lack institutional backing.
